title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TNF, wounding cues, or EGF), then perform ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac at multiple time points after withdrawal, including weeks later. Persistent AP-1 motif-containing open regions that outlast the stimulus, and that are not in naive cells, would indicate an epigenetic memory footprint.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to test necessity for maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/auxin) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after the stimulus has ended. Then measure whether memory accessibility and faster or stronger transcriptional re-induction on restimulation are lost. Removal during maintenance but not priming would show that AP-1 is needed to sustain memory, not only to establish it.

title: Re-stimulation response assay at single-cell resolution
description: Prime cells, rest them for varying durations, then restimulate and compare naive and primed cells by scRNA-seq or live reporters of AP-1 target genes. Quantify response magnitude, speed, and the fraction of responding cells, and track the decay of the memory with time and cell division. This tests whether the memory is heritable and whether it is graded or binary.

title: Sufficiency test via synthetic AP-1 induction and locus-specific recruitment
description: Transiently express FOS/JUN, or recruit them with dCas9 to a defined enhancer, in naive cells. Then test whether chromatin opening, pioneer-like nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment), and later enhanced gene responses persist after the factor is removed. Comparing this with a DNA-binding or transactivation mutant controls for specificity.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or AP-1 activity reporters in single cells through priming, rest and restimulation, and follow daughter cells. Correlate pulse history, dynamics and dimer composition with later responsiveness. This shows whether memory is stored in AP-1 levels, persistent feedback loops, or chromatin state that is inherited across divisions.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (priming assay)
description: Expose cells to a brief inflammatory or growth-factor stimulus, let them rest for days to weeks, then re-stimulate and measure faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes (RNA-seq, nascent transcription via PRO-seq) relative to naive cells. Persistence beyond the decay of FOS/JUN protein and mRNA would distinguish true memory from lingering signaling.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy profiling
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 ChIP at time points before, during and long after stimulation to find enhancers that stay open or bound after the stimulus is gone. Motif analysis and footprinting would test whether AP-1 binding marks the retained 'memory' regions, and whether the regions overlap with those showing enhanced re-induction.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 factors to deplete AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only during the rest period, then re-challenge. If memory needs AP-1 only for establishment, versus for maintenance, the timing of loss will show which, and whether chromatin accessibility persists without it.

title: Sufficiency test via synthetic AP-1 pulse and site-specific recruitment
description: Induce a transient pulse of an AP-1 factor (optogenetic or chemically inducible c-Jun/FOS) in the absence of the natural stimulus and test whether it alone leaves lasting accessibility and enhanced responsiveness. Complement with dCas9-targeted recruitment or motif mutation by CRISPR at individual enhancers to test whether AP-1 sites at a locus are necessary and sufficient for its memory.

title: Single-cell and lineage tracking of memory inheritance
description: Combine live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity or target genes with single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) and lineage barcoding to ask whether memory is carried through cell divisions and is heterogeneous across clones. Comparing sister cells, and the number of divisions after the stimulus, would show if memory is stable, heritable and cell-autonomous, versus a population-level or paracrine effect.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge, mapped by ATAC/CUT&RUN
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, TGF-β, or inflammatory signal), withdraw it for days to weeks, then re-stimulate. Compare chromatin accessibility, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, and transcription at primed versus naive cells to see whether AP-1-bound sites stay open and give a faster or stronger second response.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use inducible degron or dominant-negative (A-FOS) systems to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only after stimulus withdrawal. If memory needs AP-1 to be established but not maintained, or needs it throughout, the two timings will show that and separate initiation from maintenance.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing of memory persistence
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC on primed cells across time and through cell divisions, with barcodes or clonal tracking. This tests whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression are inherited by daughter cells and whether memory is heterogeneous (bimodal) or graded.

title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1-dependent enhancers
description: Use CRISPR deletion of AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-KRAB/dCas9-p300 at candidate memory enhancers. Measure whether disabling a motif abolishes the primed response and whether forced activation can substitute for the priming stimulus, which would show that the sites themselves carry the memory.

title: Live-cell AP-1 dynamics and reporter readout
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter, in single cells across repeated stimuli. Test whether the memory shows up as a persistent protein level, a change in dynamics, or a faster reporter induction, and whether it depends on cooperating factors or histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) checked by ChIP or CUT&Tag.

title: Stimulus-memory chromatin accessibility time course
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) with a transient signal, then run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac at multiple time points after washout. Persistent AP-1-bound enhancers that stay open after the signal ends, and that prime a faster or stronger response to restimulation, would support a memory role.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during priming versus recall
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS or JUN, or a dominant-negative A-FOS, to remove AP-1 either during the initial priming stimulus or only during the memory (washout) phase. If depleting it only during the washout phase erases enhanced re-induction, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory, not just to establish it.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of history-dependent responses
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on naive, primed and re-stimulated cells, and correlate AP-1 motif accessibility with each cell's transcriptional response. Include live reporters of AP-1 activity to link individual cells' stimulation history to their later response and to test whether memory is heritable across divisions.

title: Optogenetic or synthetic AP-1 pulse-encoding experiments
description: Drive AP-1 with controlled pulses of different duration, frequency and amplitude, using optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN. Measure target-gene output and enhancer state after later challenges to determine whether AP-1 dynamics are integrated and stored, and whether the memory is dose- or timing-dependent.

title: Pioneer-like function and locus-specific causal tests
description: Use CRISPR deletion or dCas9 perturbation of AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Pair this with in vitro nucleosome-binding assays and Hi-C or Micro-C to test whether AP-1 binding opens chromatin, recruits SWI/SNF (BAF) and sustains looping after the signal is gone. Compare the effects with those of non-AP-1 memory mechanisms, such as histone marks or DNA methylation.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury signals), wash it out, then re-stimulate after varying delays (hours to weeks). Measure whether transcriptional output and kinetics of AP-1 targets differ from naive cells, and whether the effect depends on prior AP-1 activity.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 binding profiling
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac at time points before, during, and long after the stimulus. Test whether AP-1-dependent enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and whether motif-containing sites show persistent accessibility.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use inducible dominant-negative (A-FOS), degron-tagged JUN/FOS, or CRISPRi to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only after it. If memory requires AP-1 only for establishment, it should persist after late removal; if AP-1 is also needed for maintenance, the memory should be lost.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenous fluorescent reporters of FOS/JUN activity and target-gene transcription (e.g., MS2) in single cells through stimulus, rest, and division. Test whether the history of a cell's AP-1 pulses predicts its later response, and whether the state is inherited by daughter cells in a heritable, bistable manner.

title: Targeted enhancer editing and epigenome manipulation
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or use dCas9 to recruit or block chromatin modifiers there. Then measure the effect on persistent accessibility, histone marks, and the enhanced secondary response. This tests whether AP-1 binding at specific loci is causally required for memory, rather than merely correlated with it.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating signal (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), wait days to weeks after AP-1 activity returns to baseline, then re-stimulate and measure whether transcriptional output (RNA-seq, target gene induction kinetics) is faster or stronger than in naive cells. Include dose and duration series to define the memory window.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy profiling
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN/ChIP-seq for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac across a time course (before, during, and long after stimulation) to test whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself is no longer active. Motif footprinting and single-cell multiome data can reveal whether persistent accessibility is AP-1-dependent and heterogeneous across cells.

title: Acute degron or dominant-negative perturbation at distinct phases
description: Use an inducible degron (e.g., dTAG/AID on JUN/FOS) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus (to test for establishment) or after stimulation but before re-challenge (to test for maintenance). Comparing the two shows whether AP-1 is required to write the memory, to keep it, or both.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporters
description: Track endogenous FOS/JUN with fluorescent knock-ins and AP-1 target reporters over many days in single cells and their lineages to ask whether past activity history predicts later response and whether states are inherited through division. Lineage-correlation and mother–daughter analyses separate cell-autonomous heritable memory from persistent external signaling.

title: Targeted enhancer editing and epigenetic perturbation
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or dCas9-based writers or erasers (e.g., KRAB, p300, TET) to alter their chromatin state. Then test whether memory of the prior stimulus is lost or conferred. This establishes causal links between specific AP-1 sites, chromatin changes, and the memory phenotype, while controlling for cell cycle and for other transcription factors using cell-cycle-synchronized and parallel-lineage controls.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed recall of chromatin accessibility
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a brief AP-1-activating stimulus (TPA, EGF, or injury cue), wash out, and after days to weeks profile ATAC-seq and H3K27ac CUT&Tag. Then restimulate and test whether the sites that stayed open or were primed show faster or stronger transcription (nascent RNA-seq) than naive cells.

title: Acute degron-based AP-1 depletion at different time windows
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on FOS, JUN or the pioneer-like AP-1 factors to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus, after it, or only during recall. If memory needs ongoing AP-1, removal after the priming phase should erase it. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, removal at that point should have no effect.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of lineage-linked memory
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq, with lineage barcodes or live reporters, on cells at several times after a transient stimulus. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression are inherited across cell divisions in clonal families, and whether they are bimodal, as expected for epigenetic memory.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 dynamics and target reporters
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a transcriptional reporter of a target gene (MS2/PP7) through repeated pulses of stimulation. Quantify whether the history of pulses, such as their number or spacing, changes later binding dwell times or burst frequency, which would indicate a memory beyond simple signaling.

title: Targeted epigenome editing at AP-1-dependent enhancers
description: Use dCas9 tools to either block AP-1 motifs or force chromatin opening or closing (dCas9-p300, dCas9-KRAB) at selected primed enhancers, with and without prior stimulation. Measure whether the enhancer's state is sufficient to reproduce or abolish the memory response, which separates the contribution of AP-1 binding from that of downstream chromatin marks.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or stress), wash out, then re-challenge after days to weeks. Compare transcriptional output and AP-1 occupancy with naive cells to test whether a persistent, stimulus-independent change in responsiveness exists.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 binding profiling
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag/ChIP-seq for FOS/JUN family members, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at multiple time points before, during, and long after stimulation. Test whether AP-1-dependent accessible 'memory' regions stay open after AP-1 itself returns to baseline, and whether motif-bearing sites predict this.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation (degron/dominant-negative) at different phases
description: Use an inducible degron or dominant-negative (e.g., A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the memory/maintenance phase. Distinguish AP-1 as an initiator of memory (needed only early) from a maintainer (needed continuously) by assessing chromatin state and re-challenge response.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics with lineage tracking
description: Image fluorescent reporters of endogenous FOS/JUN levels or AP-1 activity in single cells through stimulation and division, tracking lineages. Test whether history-dependent AP-1 dynamics are inherited by daughter cells and correlate with future response heterogeneity, beyond what is explained by noise.

title: Targeted motif editing and epigenome manipulation at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or dCas9-based recruitment of AP-1 factors or chromatin modifiers, and measure the effect on retained accessibility and faster re-induction of nearby genes. This tests sufficiency and necessity of AP-1 binding at individual loci for encoding memory, and extends to in vivo contexts such as wound-healing or immune-trained cells.

title: Transient stimulus, then long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a brief stimulus such as TNF, TPA, or injury signals, then run ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at multiple time points after washout. Persistence of AP-1 motif-enriched accessible sites and H3K27ac long after AP-1 activity returns to baseline would indicate a memory imprint.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or dominant-negative block during priming versus recall
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the initial priming stimulus or only during the later restimulation. If depletion at priming abolishes the enhanced secondary response but depletion at recall does not, AP-1 is needed to write the memory rather than just to read it.

title: Single-cell multiome with live AP-1 reporters
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling with a live-cell AP-1 activity reporter or FOS/JUN imaging to link each cell's history of AP-1 dynamics to its later chromatin state and transcriptional response. This tests whether the memory is cell-autonomous, heritable across divisions, and dependent on the dose or duration of the earlier AP-1 signal.

title: Motif editing and synthetic AP-1 site perturbation at candidate memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or deletion to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers that stay accessible after priming, and use dCas9-based activators or repressors to manipulate those loci. Then measure whether faster or stronger gene reactivation upon restimulation depends on the sites, which would show that they are causally required for memory.

title: Pioneer and cofactor dependence plus mitotic inheritance of AP-1 binding
description: Test whether AP-1 together with partners such as the BAF/SWI-SNF complex maintains accessibility through DNA replication and mitosis. Use synchronized cell cycles, mitotic bookmarking assays (mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN or imaging), and BAF inhibitors or degraders to determine whether the memory is epigenetically inherited and depends on AP-1 recruiting remodelers.

title: Stimulus-history chromatin accessibility time course
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient stimulus such as TPA, serum, or LPS, then profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at multiple times after washout and re-stimulation. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a memory-like imprint.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degrons or dominant-negative A-FOS to deplete AP-1 either during priming or after priming but before the second stimulus. If the primed state needs AP-1 only during establishment, it is a trigger. If it needs AP-1 during maintenance and recall, AP-1 is a continuing memory component.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of memory
description: Run paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq on primed versus naive cells before and after a second challenge, and relate AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) to the strength of the secondary transcriptional response in each cell. Test whether memory is cell-autonomous, heritable across divisions, and graded or binary.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter with lineage tracing
description: Image a FOS/JUN endogenous-tagged or AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells through repeated stimulation and cell divisions, using lineage tracking. Measure whether prior activation history, and its inheritance by daughter cells, predicts the amplitude or kinetics of later responses.

title: Targeted enhancer perturbation and epigenetic editing
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers by CRISPR base editing, or use dCas9-based writers and erasers of H3K27ac and H3K4me1 at those sites. Then measure how primed accessibility, cofactor recruitment (BAF, p300), and the faster secondary transcription change, to show whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient for the retained state.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), let signaling return to baseline, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional output and chromatin accessibility to naive cells to test for primed, enhanced responses.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin state
description: Track AP-1 factor binding (FOS, JUN, FOSL) and accessibility plus H3K27ac/H3K4me1 at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers before, during, and long after stimulation. Persistent accessibility or histone marks after AP-1 binding is lost would indicate AP-1 establishes a lasting epigenetic memory.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 during stimulus versus memory phase
description: Use dTAG/auxin-degron or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the later maintenance period. This separates AP-1's role in writing memory (needed only initially) from maintaining it (needed continuously).

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Use fluorescent reporters of AP-1 activity and endogenously tagged FOS/JUN to follow single cells and their lineages through stimulation and division. Quantify whether activity history predicts later responses and whether the state is inherited across cell divisions, indicating bistability or feedback.

title: Motif mutation and synthetic enhancer tests with in vivo validation
description: Use CRISPR to edit or delete AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or use dCas9-based tethering of AP-1/chromatin modifiers, and measure the effect on memory-associated accessibility and re-stimulation response. Complement with in vivo models such as epidermal wound or inflammation paradigms with lineage tracing to test relevance in tissue.

title: Pheromone-trail decay: AP-1 occupancy half-life after stimulus withdrawal
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury cytokines, or optogenetic ERK), then track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility and enhancer H3K27ac by time-course CUT&Tag/ATAC over days to weeks. Memory is supported if AP-1-marked sites persist well beyond the decay of AP-1 protein and transcription, and the persistence is selective for previously stimulated sites rather than a general slow decay.

title: Slightly-wrong-key test: dose and dominant-negative titration of AP-1 at the priming and recall steps
description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS or inducible dominant-negative A-FOS (or partial-affinity motif variants) to deplete or weaken AP-1 only during priming, only during the rest period, or only at re-challenge. If AP-1 is needed only at priming to establish the memory but not at recall, it is an initiator, while a requirement at recall means it is a reader. Partial or mismatched motif variants should show whether graded AP-1 input produces graded memory.

title: Moiré test: combinatorial dimer and cofactor composition of memory sites
description: Profile which FOS/JUN/ATF dimers and partner factors (e.g., pioneer factors such as BAF or lineage TFs) occupy primed versus naive enhancers using sequential ChIP (re-ChIP) or CUT&RUN with single-molecule footprinting. Test whether memory is carried by the specific combinations that emerge on chromatin after priming, which neither AP-1 nor the partners show alone.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory inheritance
description: Combine live reporters of AP-1 activity with barcoded lineage tracing and multiome (scRNA and scATAC) so sister cells can be compared after priming and several divisions. High sister-cell concordance of recall-response magnitude, and of accessibility at AP-1 sites, that exceeds that of unrelated cells would show heritable, cell-autonomous memory, while discordance would indicate transient signaling states.

title: Sufficiency by site-specific rewriting and erasure
description: Use dCas9-based tools to deposit or remove AP-1 motifs or AP-1 recruitment at chosen enhancers (e.g., motif deletion by base editing, or dCas9-FOS recruitment) in naive and primed cells. Test whether deleting motifs erases the faster or stronger re-response at that locus, and whether artificially recruiting AP-1 to a naive locus is enough to install a memory-like response without the original stimulus.

title: Rope-style distributed memory: single-site vs. combinatorial AP-1 motif disruption
description: Borrowing the rope that is strong because no fiber spans the whole length: test whether memory is held by overlapping, partially redundant AP-1 sites rather than any single enhancer. Use CRISPR base-editing of AP-1 motifs singly and in combinations at stimulus-primed loci, then measure the decay time of the enhanced re-response after the stimulus is withdrawn, to see whether persistence scales with the number of sites instead of depending on any one.

title: Starter-culture transfer: inherited AP-1 state without the original stimulus
description: Following the sourdough starter that is inherited and never started, ask whether the AP-1 chromatin state can propagate without the original signal. Sort primed cells, withdraw the stimulus, and track the AP-1 occupancy, accessibility (ATAC) and H3K27ac of cell-line daughters over many divisions. Then test sufficiency by transplanting or co-culturing primed nuclei, or by nuclear transfer, into naive cells to see whether the primed response is transferred.

title: Noise as ingredient: single-cell variability in AP-1 pulses predicts memory strength
description: Treat the noise as the signal: live-image fluorescent FOS/JUN reporters and measure the pulse amplitude, frequency and duration in single cells during priming. Test whether the stochastic dynamics, and not the mean level, predict each cell's later hyper-responsiveness, using optogenetic AP-1 induction with matched means but different noise structures.

title: Slime-mold abandonment: tracking which AP-1-opened sites are later retracted
description: Inspired by the slime mold abandoning a tunnel it just built, map the full lifecycle of AP-1-dependent enhancers with time-resolved CUT&RUN and ATAC after priming, and separate sites that persist (memory candidates) from those that are opened and then abandoned. Then ask whether the persistent subset has distinctive motif spacing, pioneer partners (e.g., BAF/SWI-SNF) or histone marks, and test it with degron-mediated (dTAG) AP-1 removal at different times after priming to determine when AP-1 is required to maintain the site versus only to establish it.

title: Negative results in a bottle: delayed re-challenge and AP-1 loss after long intervals
description: Borrowing the negative result mailed to the wrong decade, run re-stimulation at intervals from hours to months, in vitro and in vivo (e.g., skin or immune stem cells), after acute AP-1 inhibition or degradation during the quiescent interval. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, loss of AP-1 at the time of re-challenge but not in the interval, and vice versa, should dissociate storage from recall. Record also the cases where the memory does not appear, as bounds on its duration and cell-type specificity.

title: Lip-shaving the memory: tuning AP-1 at enhancer edges, not the core factor
description: Inspired by tuning a bell at its lip rather than its crown: instead of knocking out FOS/JUN (the crown), use CRISPR base-editing or dCas9 perturbation of individual AP-1 motifs and their flanking sequence at stimulus-primed enhancers, then re-stimulate after a rest period. If memory resides in specific sites, edits there should alter the secondary response (faster/stronger re-induction) without changing the primary response.

title: Negative-space footprinting of the 'key' after the signal is gone
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, injury, or neuronal activity) and washout, run time-course ATAC/CUT&Tag/DNase footprinting for AP-1 occupancy, together with H3K27ac and H3K4me1, to map sites that stay open or marked once AP-1 itself has left. Combine this with acute degron depletion (dTAG) of JUN/FOS at different times to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish, to maintain, or only to read out the memory.

title: Dead-reckoning reporters: single-cell lineage-tracked history of AP-1 dynamics
description: Live-image AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN reporters or optogenetic input) in single cells with lineage tracking through a first stimulus, a rest period spanning several divisions, and a second stimulus. Regress the second response on the cell's own past pulse history and on its relatives' histories, to separate heritable memory from cell-to-cell noise or a persistent signal.

title: Optogenetic pulse-code writing and erasing of memory
description: Drive AP-1 with light-controlled FOS/JUN or an upstream kinase using defined pulse frequency, duration, and number, then measure the second response after varying delays. Mapping which input codes leave a durable trace, and which patterns (e.g., opposing inputs or chromatin-opener inhibitors) erase it, gives a causal input-output test with a built-in null of identical total dose delivered as one continuous pulse.

title: Cross-context natural experiments: AP-1 memory in primed vs naive cells in vivo
description: Compare AP-1 motif accessibility and transcriptional response in cells with documented history, such as trained-immunity macrophages, post-injury epithelial 'wound memory' stem cells, and activity-experienced neurons, against naive counterparts with matched age and cell type. Use single-cell multiome data and AP-1 dependency (e.g., dominant-negative A-FOS) to ask whether the memory is consistently AP-1-dependent across tissues or specific to some.

title: Shaken-ratchet pulse-history test
description: Use optogenetic or chemically gated AP-1 (e.g., FOS/JUN) activation with identical total dose but different pulse frequencies, noise levels and spacing, then measure ATAC-seq accessibility and enhancer-gene output after a washout of weeks. If AP-1 acts as a memory mechanism, the retained chromatin state should depend on pulse pattern and history rather than on total dose, and should show a threshold or ratchet-like response.

title: Acute degron removal after the stimulus (maintenance vs. initiation)
description: After a priming stimulus (e.g., inflammation, injury, or differentiation cue), deplete JUN/FOS/ATF with a dTAG or auxin degron at staggered times and measure whether primed accessibility and the faster secondary transcriptional response persist. Memory that is stored in chromatin should persist after AP-1 is removed, whereas memory that needs continuous AP-1 occupancy should decay at a rate that tracks its depletion.

title: Dead-layer footprinting: AP-1 motif sites that stay open without AP-1
description: Compare primed and naive cells by CUT&Tag/ChIP for AP-1, pioneer-like partners (e.g., BAF), H3K27ac and H3K4me1, together with ATAC and footprinting, at various times after the stimulus. Classify the sites where AP-1 binding is lost but accessibility or histone marks remain as an inherited 'scaffold' layer, then test with CRISPRi or motif mutation whether those sites cause the faster re-response.

title: Single-cell lineage-barcoded inheritance of AP-1 state
description: Combine clonal barcoding with multiome (scRNA and scATAC) sequencing and live AP-1 reporters, and compare sister cells and clones across several divisions after the stimulus. Heritability of the AP-1 accessibility state, estimated from the correlation within clones relative to random pairs, together with its decay half-life in generations rather than time, would separate true mitotic memory from persistent signaling.

title: Cheap-noise perturbation of the AP-1 circuit to map memory basins
description: Inject controlled noise (variable dose of stimulus, or tunable expression of a dominant-negative such as A-FOS) into primed cells, then quantify the bimodality and hysteresis of the AP-1 target response using flow or imaging reporters in a dose-up versus dose-down sweep. A hysteresis loop, with cells that stay in the primed basin at identical input, would show bistable self-reinforcement. Fitting the data with a model would tell us whether AP-1 positive feedback (JUN autoregulation) is sufficient or whether chromatin must be included.

title: Shave the inside: degron-titrated AP-1 removal after the stimulus ends
description: Instead of perturbing the inducing signal (the 'outside'), use an acute degron (dTAG/AID) on FOS/JUN family members at graded times after a transient stimulus (e.g., wound, cytokine, or stress) and ask whether chromatin accessibility and the enhanced re-response persist without AP-1. If AP-1 is truly a memory mechanism, there should be a window where it is needed to write the memory but dispensable to maintain it, or the reverse; the shape of that window distinguishes memory writer from maintainer.

title: Kintsugi test: AP-1 motif edits at sites made accessible by prior stimulation
description: Use CRISPR base editing or saturating mutagenesis at enhancers that gain accessibility after a first stimulus (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) to ablate single AP-1 motifs, then re-stimulate after rest and measure transcription (PRO-seq/reporter). Sites where a motif break abolishes faster/stronger secondary induction while leaving the naive first response intact identify the 'fracture' that is load-bearing for memory, not for response.

title: Auction where the loser pays: competition between AP-1 dimers and pioneer/other factors at memory loci
description: Titrate the levels of different AP-1 dimer compositions (FOS/JUN/ATF, with dominant-negative A-FOS as a decoy) and measure occupancy competition with other factors (e.g., nucleosome, STAT, NF-κB) by single-molecule footprinting or Fiber-seq on the same DNA molecules. Memory should show up as sites where the 'loser' state (a factor-displaced or nucleosome-occluded state) leaves a lasting cost, i.e., a persistent footprint after AP-1 itself leaves.

title: Moiré readout: single-cell multiome lineage-tracked comparison of two stimulus histories
description: Subject clonal cells (barcoded) to two regular stimulus trains (e.g., pulses with different periods) and use paired scRNA/ATAC plus live AP-1 reporters (FOS-HaloTag/JUN) to see whether the emergent third pattern, a clone-specific response not predictable from either train alone, is inherited across divisions. Heritability of the interference pattern within clones versus between clones, with AP-1 occupancy as the mediator, tests whether memory is carried by AP-1 state rather than by lineage noise.

title: Mycelial-delay test: the lag is the computation, so measure slow AP-1 dynamics and nucleosome turnover
description: Perform time-resolved CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors, H3K27ac, and a nucleosome-turnover/histone-age label (e.g., SNAP-tag pulse-chase) across days after a transient stimulus, then fit models in which the delay between AP-1 loss and enhancer decay is the memory timescale. Then test causality by optogenetically or chemically prolonging AP-1 activity for a short window and checking whether the persistence time scales with it, which would show that the delay encodes the history.

title: Self-repelling "I was here" footprint: AP-1 accessibility after stimulus washout
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), then track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for AP-1 motif sites, H3K27ac) over days to weeks after Fos/Jun levels return to baseline. Persistence of AP-1-dependent accessible 'scars' at the same loci, which then give faster or stronger transcription on restimulation, would show memory is stored in the chromatin footprint rather than in ongoing AP-1 activity.

title: Acute degradation timing: is AP-1 needed to write, hold, or read the memory?
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons or dominant-negative A-Fos to remove AP-1 at three distinct times: during priming, during the rest interval, and during restimulation. If loss during priming abolishes the memory but loss during rest or recall does not, AP-1 is a writer only. If loss during rest erases it, AP-1 must keep maintaining it.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of primed vs naive response with live AP-1 reporters
description: Combine live Fos/Jun reporters or a FosTRAP-style recombinase label with barcoded lineages, so sister cells can be compared after a first stimulus and a later challenge. High sister-cell concordance of the second response, which persists through division, would indicate heritable memory and separate it from noise or persistent signaling.

title: Site-specific motif editing and dCas9 perturbation at memory enhancers
description: Identify loci that show primed responses, then mutate individual AP-1 motifs by base editing, or recruit dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-p300, and test whether the memory of the loci is lost or created without altering the global AP-1 level. Doing this across many motifs (e.g., a massively parallel reporter assay in primed vs naive cells) tests whether the memory is sequence-encoded and whether AP-1 cooperates with partners such as BAF or pioneer factors.

title: Dose, interval and decay-curve mapping with mathematical modeling of memory kinetics
description: Vary the number, spacing and strength of stimulus pulses (including irregular intervals), and measure response amplitude and AP-1 binding at each. Fit models comparing a mechanism with no memory, one with a slowly decaying chromatin state, and one with bistability. The model that is best supported, such as hysteresis or a half-life much longer than AP-1 protein turnover, would show whether AP-1 behaves like a memory device and over what timescale.

title: Selective subtraction test (inner-lip shaving)
description: Mechanism borrowed from bell tuning: the state is set by removing material, not adding it. Instead of overexpressing AP-1, use acute degron-mediated removal (dTAG/AID of FOS/JUN family members, or dominant-negative A-Fos) at defined times after a transient stimulus, and measure whether the primed transcriptional response and chromatin accessibility at AP-1 sites persist, decay, or collapse. This tests whether AP-1 is required to maintain the memory or only to establish it.

title: Memory read out from the 'failed' sites (losing-bid information)
description: Mechanism borrowed from auctions: the information is in the bids that lose. After a first stimulus, use ATAC/CUT&RUN for AP-1 and pioneer-factor co-binding to identify motifs that were occupied or opened but did NOT lead to transcription (poised or non-productive sites). Test whether these silent-but-marked sites predict the magnitude of a second-stimulus response better than the sites that were active, using held-out genes and a predictive model.

title: Misalignment interference test (moiré)
description: Mechanism borrowed from moiré: a pattern emerges only from slight offset between two regular structures, so it reveals offsets invisible in either alone. Present two stimuli with varied timing and dose offsets (e.g., pulsed ERK/JNK inputs with different periods) while live-imaging AP-1 reporters and FOS/JUN dynamics at single-cell level. Look for beat-like interference in the second response that depends on the offset, which would show history-dependent encoding in AP-1 dynamics rather than simple state.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory persistence
description: Barcode or live-track cells through a stimulus, and let them divide without stimulus. Use sister-cell concordance of AP-1 target expression and accessibility, versus random pairs, over several divisions to quantify heritability and half-life. Pair with mitotic bookmarking assays (live imaging and CUT&RUN on mitotic chromosomes) to see whether AP-1 stays bound through mitosis.

title: Sufficiency by site-specific rewriting
description: Use CRISPR to mutate individual AP-1 motifs (or dCas9-based recruitment and displacement of AP-1) at a few endogenous enhancers whose primed state is known. Then test whether memory of the prior stimulus at that locus is lost while neighbouring loci keep it. Combine with an orthogonal epigenetic readout (H3K27ac, nucleosome remodeling by BAF) to determine whether AP-1 itself or downstream chromatin marks carry the memory.

title: Prior-stimulus ATAC/CUT&Tag time course with AP-1 degron
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts with LPS, TNF, or wounding signals), wash out, and track chromatin accessibility, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and H3K27ac at 'latent' enhancers for days to weeks. Test necessity by acutely degrading (dTAG/AID) AP-1 factors at different times: before the first stimulus (is it needed to write memory?) versus after it (is it needed to maintain memory?).

title: Re-stimulation response kinetics as a memory readout
description: Challenge primed versus naive cells with a second stimulus after varying rest intervals, and measure the transcriptional response (bulk or scRNA-seq, nascent RNA via PRO-seq) for faster, stronger or qualitatively different induction. Compare AP-1 site mutants (CRISPR editing of motifs at specific enhancers) or dominant-negative A-FOS with wild type to show that the primed response depends on AP-1 and to measure the memory half-life.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics with heritability analysis
description: Use endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and an AP-1 reporter to follow lineages through divisions, quantifying pulse frequency, amplitude and the dynamics of a reporter gene. Treat cell-to-cell variability as signal: test whether sister cells' AP-1 history correlates with each other's re-response beyond what shared lineage alone predicts. Comparing correlation decay over generations to that of shuffled controls estimates mitotic heritability.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 pulses and optogenetic writing
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemogenetic control (e.g., light-gated JUN/FOS, or a stimulus-free dCas9-activator at AP-1 sites), varying pulse duration, frequency and dose in the absence of any natural stimulus. Then measure whether chromatin opening and enhanced re-response persist after AP-1 is turned off, and which pulse patterns are encoded, to separate AP-1 as a writer of memory from a passive reader of other marks.

title: Cooperating-factor and chromatin-remodeler dependency mapping
description: Combine CUT&RUN/ChIP-seq, Micro-C or Hi-C and proteomics (BioID) for AP-1 and its partners (BAF/SWI-SNF, pioneer factors, ATF/CEBP/ETS) at memory-bearing enhancers, then perturb the partners with CRISPR screens or inhibitors. Determine whether memory persists via AP-1 occupancy itself, via remodeler-deposited nucleosome changes or histone marks that outlast AP-1, or via self-reinforcing feedback such as AP-1 inducing its own genes (FOS, JUN), by testing which layer is lost first after AP-1 loss.

title: Prime-and-rechallenge with chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a transient stimulus such as TPA, wounding cytokines, or EGF, then wash out and rechallenge days to weeks later. Use ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and H3K27ac to test whether AP-1-dependent enhancers stay open after the stimulus ends and whether they drive faster or stronger transcription on the second exposure.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined time points
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on FOS, JUN, or FOSL family members, or a dominant-negative A-FOS, to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during the memory (post-stimulus) phase. If memory needs AP-1 only to establish it, loss during priming would abolish it, while loss during the memory phase would show whether AP-1 must also maintain it. Compare the outcome by RNA-seq and accessibility.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage-resolved memory tracking
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on primed and naive populations over time, with barcoded lineage tracing, to see whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target gene expression persist in daughter cells through divisions. Heritability of the state within clones, compared with the variance between clones, would show whether it is truly mitotically stable memory or only long-lived signaling.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity and dynamics
description: Combine AP-1 transcriptional reporters, endogenous tagging of FOS/JUN, and optogenetic or pulsed stimulation with time-lapse imaging. Measure how long activity persists, whether it shows hysteresis or bistability, and whether the response to a second pulse depends on the interval and history of the first.

title: Causal enhancer perturbation and pioneer-factor tests
description: Use dCas9-based epigenome editing, motif mutation, or CRISPR deletion of specific AP-1-bound memory enhancers to test whether they are required for faster re-induction of nearby genes. Pair this with ectopic AP-1 recruitment or induction at naive loci, and with measures of cooperating pioneer factors and histone modifiers (e.g., BAF/SWI-SNF, p300), to determine whether AP-1 is sufficient to establish a heritable open state rather than just correlating with it.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells to a brief AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then run longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac at days to weeks after withdrawal. Persistent AP-1 motif-enriched accessible regions after the stimulus has cleared, and not in naive cells, would indicate AP-1-dependent epigenetic memory.

title: Acute degron-based depletion at distinct time windows
description: Use auxin- or dTAG-inducible degradation of AP-1 components (e.g., FOS, JUNB, or dominant-negative A-FOS) during the priming phase versus the maintenance phase, then challenge cells with a second stimulus. If depletion during priming abolishes the enhanced secondary response but depletion during maintenance does not, AP-1 is needed to establish but not maintain memory, and the reverse pattern would show it is needed for maintenance.

title: Primed vs. naive re-stimulation transcriptional response
description: Compare RNA-seq and nascent transcription (PRO-seq/TT-seq) after a first versus second stimulus, with varying rest intervals between them, in wild-type and AP-1-perturbed cells. Faster or stronger induction of the same genes on re-challenge, with a decay constant that depends on AP-1 dosage, would quantify memory strength and duration.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell reporter of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Combine single-cell RNA+ATAC with live imaging of fluorescent AP-1 activity reporters (or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN) and lineage tracing, to follow primed cells through divisions. Heritable inheritance of AP-1 state and accessibility in daughter cells, and correlation between a cell's past AP-1 activity and its later response, would show whether memory is cell-autonomous and mitotically stable.

title: Site-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 motifs at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base editing or deletion of AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, along with dCas9-based recruitment or blockade of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers like BAF, then test whether accessibility persistence and enhanced re-induction are lost. Also test sufficiency by inserting AP-1 sites into a naive locus and examining whether it retains accessibility after transient AP-1 activation, to separate AP-1 as a driver from AP-1 as a passive marker.

title: Transient stimulus, delayed re-challenge with chromatin profiling
description: Expose cells to a defined stimulus (e.g., TNF, serum, or wounding), let them rest until AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare transcription and ATAC-seq accessibility with naive cells. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open, and whether the primed genes respond faster or more strongly.

title: CUT&RUN/ChIP-seq time course of AP-1 occupancy and enhancer marks
description: Map FOS/JUN/FOSL binding, H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and BAF (SWI/SNF) complex occupancy before, during, and long after stimulation. If AP-1 acts as memory, residual accessible 'latent' enhancers should persist after AP-1 itself has left, and the sites that remain should be enriched for AP-1 motifs.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 at different phases
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the memory/maintenance period. If AP-1 is needed to establish memory but not to maintain it, you would see lost priming only with early depletion. Maintenance dependence would show up as loss of the memory response with late depletion.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of memory and heterogeneity
description: Do paired scRNA/scATAC-seq, or live imaging of AP-1 reporters, across stimulation, rest and restimulation. Test whether individual cells that had high AP-1 activity retain accessibility and respond more strongly, and whether the state is inherited through cell divisions in lineage-traced clones.

title: Motif-specific synthetic perturbation of enhancers
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or delete AP-1 motifs at specific memory-associated enhancers, or use dCas9 to recruit or block AP-1 there. Test the effect on retained accessibility and on the faster secondary response at the linked genes. Combine with reporter assays to show that the AP-1 site is necessary, and that adding it to a naive enhancer is sufficient, to produce memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., TNF, EGF, or wounding) transiently, then perform ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN), H3K27ac, and H3K4me1 at days 0, 1, 7, and 28 after washout. Persistent AP-1-motif-enriched accessible regions in the absence of ongoing signaling, versus naive cells, would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate maintenance from initiation
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on JUN/FOS or ATF family members, or a dominant-negative like A-FOS, at different times: before the priming stimulus, during the memory phase, and before re-stimulation. Compare chromatin state and transcriptional response to determine whether AP-1 is required to establish memory, to maintain it, or to execute faster re-induction.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics and single-cell heterogeneity
description: Compare primed versus naive cells upon second stimulus using time-resolved scRNA-seq, nascent RNA (PRO-seq/TT-seq), and live reporters of AP-1 target genes. Faster, stronger, or more frequent induction in primed cells that depends on AP-1 binding site integrity would show memory, and single-cell data can distinguish stable bistable states from graded changes.

title: Targeted enhancer editing and synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely use dCas9-based tethering of FOS/JUN to a naive locus. Test if motif loss abolishes retained accessibility and primed response, and whether forced AP-1 recruitment alone is sufficient to create a lasting, heritable open state after the tether is removed.

title: Mitotic retention and inheritance across divisions
description: Track AP-1 occupancy and accessibility through mitosis and across multiple cell divisions using mitotic-synchronized CUT&Tag, live-cell imaging of tagged JUN/FOS, and lineage-tracked sister cells. Mitotic bookmarking by AP-1 and similar memory in sister cells would show it is heritable, and in vivo tests such as inflammation-primed epithelial or stem cells could test physiological relevance.

title: Transient stimulus with longitudinal chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding-like signals), then run ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at multiple time points, including long after the stimulus is gone. Sites that stay open and AP-1 bound after the signal clears, and that give a faster or stronger response on restimulation, would indicate a memory function.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined windows (degron)
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degradation of FOS, JUN, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, and deplete AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or only after it, during the memory period. If depletion during priming blocks later enhanced responses but depletion during the memory period does not, AP-1 is needed to establish the memory. If depletion during the memory period also erases it, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/clonal tracking
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on primed and naive populations, with barcoded lineages, to relate AP-1 motif accessibility to transcriptional output across cell divisions. This tests whether the primed state is heritable through mitosis in clonal sisters and whether it depends on AP-1 motif activity.

title: Enhancer mutagenesis and CRISPR perturbation of AP-1 sites
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or base editing to disrupt specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Then measure whether the primed accessibility, histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), and the enhanced re-induction of nearby genes are lost. Reporter or endogenous readouts would show whether the sites are causal rather than merely correlated.

title: Live-cell AP-1 dynamics and optogenetic priming
description: Track AP-1 activity in single cells with live reporters or imaging of FOS/JUN levels and binding. Combine this with optogenetic or pulsatile stimulation using different durations and frequencies, then record later responses. This shows whether the dose, duration, and history of AP-1 activity predict the strength of a later response, and whether the memory is stored in the cell state or in ongoing AP-1 signaling.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts, or keratinocytes) with a transient signal, then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at baseline, during stimulation, and after weeks of washout. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open or primed, and whether AP-1 stays bound, after the stimulus is gone.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to test necessity for maintenance
description: Use a degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) either during the priming phase or only during the memory phase. Measure whether the enhanced secondary transcriptional response and the accessibility at primed sites are lost, which separates AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

title: Single-cell multiome with live reporter lineage tracing
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC with an AP-1 activity reporter (e.g., a TRE-driven fluorescent protein) to follow clones through stimulation and rest. Test whether the memory state is heritable across divisions and whether it is bimodal or graded, and whether the reporter history predicts the strength of the recall response.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment sufficiency test
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment of FOS/JUN, or insert AP-1 motifs, at a naive locus, with and without pioneer factor co-binding. Test whether transient AP-1 occupancy alone creates persistent accessibility, histone marks (H3K27ac/H3K4me1), and a faster re-induction, and whether motif mutations at endogenous memory enhancers abolish it.

title: Epigenetic-mechanism coupling and mathematical modeling
description: Measure histone modifications, DNA methylation and BAF/SWI-SNF occupancy at AP-1 memory sites, and inhibit these factors (e.g., BRG1 or p300 inhibitors) during the rest period. Then fit kinetic models of AP-1 binding, nucleosome remodeling and feedback to the time-course data to test whether AP-1 itself carries memory or depends on a downstream chromatin state.

title: Longitudinal ATAC/CUT&Tag after transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a transient stimulus such as TPA, TNF, or wounding. Then map AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility at days to weeks after washout, and test whether AP-1-motif enhancers remain open or primed, and whether they drive faster transcription on restimulation than in naïve cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degrons or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only after it ends. If memory requires AP-1 only for establishment, degradation in the maintenance phase should leave it intact. If AP-1 is needed for maintenance, memory should decay. Read out restimulation response, accessibility, and H3K27ac.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and memory
description: Track AP-1 reporters or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN in single cells through repeated stimulation pulses. Quantify whether the history of past pulses predicts later response amplitude and kinetics, and whether the response is heritable across cell divisions in sister cells, to separate true memory from cell-to-cell heterogeneity.

title: Sufficiency test with synthetic AP-1 induction and optogenetics
description: Drive AP-1 activity with a controlled optogenetic or chemogenetic c-Jun/c-Fos system without upstream signaling. Then test whether a pulse alone creates durable accessibility and a primed transcriptional response at endogenous loci. Vary pulse duration and frequency to define the dose and timing thresholds for memory.

title: Perturbing chromatin cofactors and in vivo memory models
description: Test whether AP-1 memory depends on partner factors such as BAF/SWI-SNF, p300, or pioneer factors. Inhibit or deplete them after the initial stimulus, and use CUT&Tag and Micro-C to track enhancer-promoter contacts. Validate in vivo, for example with repeated skin injury or inflammatory challenge, by lineage tracing and by comparing a primary to a secondary response.

title: Stimulus-then-washout chromatin accessibility time course
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA, TNF, or wounding. After washout, run ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for AP-1 (FOS/JUN), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 over days to weeks to see whether newly opened enhancers stay open after AP-1 binding has decayed.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times after the stimulus
description: Use degron-tagged FOS, JUN or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the stimulus or well after it. Measure whether accessibility and the faster secondary transcriptional response persist without continuing AP-1 activity. Persistence means the memory is independent of AP-1, and loss means AP-1 maintains it.

title: Functional re-stimulation assay of primed vs. naive cells
description: Give a first stimulus, rest the cells, then give a second stimulus. Compare nascent RNA (PRO-seq or SLAM-seq) and gene induction kinetics against naive cells. Repeat with AP-1 perturbed during only the priming phase to test whether AP-1 is necessary for the enhanced or faster response.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage-tracked memory persistence
description: Run paired scATAC and scRNA-seq with live reporters of AP-1 activity, using barcoded lineage tracing across cell divisions. This tests whether accessibility states are inherited clonally, whether memory is heterogeneous or bimodal, and whether it correlates with past AP-1 activity levels.

title: Targeted synthetic AP-1 site manipulation at memory loci
description: At candidate memory enhancers, use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or use dCas9-based recruitment or blocking of AP-1 and chromatin remodelers (e.g., BAF). Test whether the motif is needed to establish memory, to maintain it, or both. Read this out with allele-specific accessibility, histone marks and reporter induction after a delay. Add in vivo validation, such as epidermal stem cell wound memory in mice.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, PMA, or wounding signals). Track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs at multiple times after washout, out to days or weeks and through cell divisions. Persistent accessibility or binding after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate memory.

title: Acute degron depletion at memory vs. naive stages
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron or dTAG on c-JUN/c-FOS or a dominant-negative (A-FOS). Deplete AP-1 either during priming or only after priming, before the re-challenge. If priming-phase loss abolishes the enhanced secondary response but later loss does not, AP-1 is needed to establish memory. If later loss also abolishes it, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporter output
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN together with an AP-1 reporter across repeated stimulations and lineage tracking. Test whether prior pulse history predicts the amplitude of the next response in individual cells and in their daughters. Compare with the history dependence of non-AP-1 reporters.

title: Enhancer-targeted epigenome editing and motif mutation
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based editing, at candidate primed enhancers. Measure whether this removes the faster or stronger transcriptional response on re-stimulation, and whether the accessibility and H3K27ac changes persist. This separates AP-1 as the cause of memory from AP-1 merely marking it.

title: Multiome profiling with pioneer-factor and cofactor perturbation
description: Run single-cell RNA plus ATAC (multiome) on primed and naive cells, and link persistent accessible regions to the response on re-challenge. Perturb the AP-1 partners and chromatin remodelers that could provide the persistence, such as BAF/SWI-SNF, and test which are required for memory. Include Hi-C or Micro-C to see whether looping is kept.

title: Transient stimulus with longitudinal chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Give cells a brief pulse of a stimulus that activates AP-1 (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), then run ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS/JUN), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 at days to weeks after washout. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a memory state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN, FOS or ATF family members, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Deplete AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or only after it, then measure whether the primed accessibility and the enhanced transcriptional response to a second stimulus persist. This separates a role for AP-1 in establishing memory from a role in maintaining it.

title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation response assay
description: Compare nascent transcription (PRO-seq or SLAM-seq) and gene induction kinetics between primed and naive cells after a second challenge. Include a gradient of rest periods and mutate or CRISPRi-silence specific AP-1 binding sites at candidate enhancers. This tests whether memory is encoded at specific AP-1-dependent loci, and how long it lasts.

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell AP-1 reporter lineage tracing
description: Use live imaging of an AP-1 activity reporter or tagged FOS/JUN, with lineage tracking through divisions. Follow with matched single-cell RNA and ATAC to link past AP-1 dynamics (pulse duration, amplitude) to later accessibility and responsiveness. This tests whether memory is heritable through mitosis and whether it is graded or all-or-none at the single-cell level.

title: Sufficiency test with synthetic AP-1 activation and chromatin-state perturbation
description: Drive AP-1 optogenetically or chemogenetically in naive cells, and in parallel use dCas9-based recruitment of AP-1 to a target locus. Then test whether this alone leaves lasting accessibility and enhanced responsiveness. Combine with inhibition of SWI/SNF (BAF) or of histone-modifying enzymes to determine which chromatin cofactors convert transient AP-1 binding into stable memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating signal (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury), let activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq) and kinetics against naive cells to see whether prior exposure primes a faster or stronger response.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility
description: Profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, motif accessibility, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) before, during, and long after stimulation. Persistent open or primed enhancers after AP-1 levels fall would indicate a chromatin-encoded memory footprint.

title: Acute AP-1 loss-of-function with timed degradation
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS or JUN, or dominant-negative A-FOS, to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the memory interval. This separates AP-1's role in establishing memory from maintaining it, and tests whether enhancer accessibility and the primed response are lost.

title: Live-cell single-cell reporters and lineage tracking
description: Image AP-1 activity with fluorescent reporters or tagged FOS/JUN in single cells after a pulse, following them and their daughters over several divisions. Test whether heterogeneous or persistent activity states are heritable and correlate with later response strength, distinguishing cell-intrinsic memory from ongoing signaling.

title: Synthetic AP-1 site editing and in vivo injury model
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and test the effect on primed responses in cells. Parallel in vivo repeat-injury or repeat-inflammation experiments, such as skin wounding, with AP-1 perturbation would test whether memory is functionally relevant in tissue.

title: Longitudinal ATAC/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then map chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints from hours to weeks after washout. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a memory-like chromatin state.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin- or dTAG-inducible degradation of FOS/JUN family members at different times: before, during, and after the priming stimulus. If depletion only during priming erases later hyper-responsiveness but depletion after priming does not, AP-1 is needed for establishing memory; if post-priming depletion also erases it, AP-1 is needed for maintenance.

title: Secondary-challenge transcriptional response assay
description: Prime cells, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure RNA-seq or nascent transcription (PRO-seq/TT-seq) versus naive cells. Compare the magnitude and kinetics of gene induction at AP-1-dependent loci, and test whether the enhanced response is lost with AP-1 motif mutation or dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS).

title: CRISPR editing of AP-1 motifs at memory enhancers
description: Mutate or delete specific AP-1 motifs at candidate primed enhancers, or use dCas9 to recruit or block AP-1 there, and then test the persistence of H3K27ac, accessibility, and re-stimulation response. This tests whether AP-1 binding at those sites is causally required for the stored state, rather than merely correlated with it.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Pair single-cell ATAC plus RNA with clonal barcoding or live reporters of AP-1 activity to follow primed cells through divisions. Test whether AP-1-linked accessibility and responsiveness are inherited by daughter cells and decay at a measurable rate, and whether memory is heterogeneous or bimodal across cells.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge, mapping AP-1 chromatin accessibility
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding, or PMA), let them rest for days to weeks, then profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN/ChIP. Persistent accessibility and AP-1 motif occupancy at 'memory' enhancers, along with faster or stronger transcription on re-challenge, would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during priming versus during memory maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS, JUN, or ATF3 to remove AP-1 either only during the priming stimulus or only after priming. If depletion at priming prevents memory but depletion afterward does not, AP-1 is needed for establishment. If depletion afterward erases memory, it is needed for maintenance.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of memory-state heritability
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq, or live imaging with AP-1 reporters, across cell divisions after priming. Lineage barcoding or sister-cell comparison would show whether AP-1-linked accessibility and expression states are inherited clonally and how long they last.

title: Pioneer-like activity and chromatin-mark analysis at AP-1 sites
description: Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1, nucleosome positioning, and BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment (e.g., BRG1 CUT&Tag) at AP-1 sites before, during, and after the stimulus. Use motif-mutated or dCas9-blocked enhancers to test whether AP-1 binding is required to leave a lasting epigenetic mark.

title: Synthetic AP-1 activation sufficiency test
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 activation (e.g., inducible FOS/JUN or a light-controlled version) in naive cells. Varying the dose and duration, then testing the response to a later stimulus, would show whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to create a persistent primed state. Compare the result with a non-AP-1 transcription factor control.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts with LPS, TNF, or wounding), then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at days to weeks after washout. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open or primed, and whether AP-1 occupancy persists, compared with naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different timepoints (dTAG/AID)
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus or only during the later memory phase. If the memory is encoded by AP-1, depleting it during the stimulus should prevent the memory. If AP-1 maintains the memory, depleting it later should erase it. Readouts are accessibility and the faster secondary-response transcription.

title: Secondary-challenge transcriptional response assay
description: Give cells a primary stimulus, rest them, then re-challenge them. Measure nascent transcription (PRO-seq/TT-seq) and RNA-seq to quantify faster or stronger induction of genes at AP-1-bound loci. Correlate the size of the memory effect with the level of retained AP-1 binding and chromatin marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1).

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of lineage-traced memory
description: Use single-cell RNA+ATAC with AP-1 motif activity inference (chromVAR) and clonal barcoding or live reporters (AP-1 activity reporter) to follow whether AP-1 history is inherited by daughter cells. Test whether past AP-1 activity predicts future accessibility and response across divisions, separating heritable states from transient noise.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and site-specific perturbation
description: Mutate or CRISPR-block individual AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or use dCas9 to recruit AP-1 or chromatin remodelers (BAF) to naive loci. Test whether the site is necessary and sufficient for establishing persistent accessibility and primed responses, and whether remodeler inhibition (BRG1) uncouples AP-1 binding from the memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed recall of chromatin accessibility
description: Expose cells to a defined pulse of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding cytokines, or mechanical stress), then wash out and let them rest for days to weeks. Re-stimulate and use ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy and accessibility to test whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and show faster or stronger transcriptional responses than in naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during priming versus recall
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN, FOS or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, and deplete AP-1 either only during the initial priming or only during the memory (rest) phase. This separates AP-1 as the initiator of memory from AP-1 as the maintainer, as shown by whether accessibility and enhanced recall persist without it.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of memory states
description: Perform paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq (with lineage barcodes) before, during, and long after stimulation to link AP-1 motif accessibility to later gene expression in the same cells and clonal lineages. This tests whether the memory is heritable across divisions and whether it is heterogeneous (bimodal) or graded.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporters
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN and use enhancer or target-gene reporters in live cells to measure AP-1 levels, binding residence time (single-molecule tracking), and reporter activity through stimulation, rest, and re-stimulation. This reveals whether memory is carried by persistent AP-1 protein or feedback loops, or by a changed chromatin state that outlasts AP-1 presence.

title: Targeted enhancer manipulation and sufficiency tests
description: Mutate or delete AP-1 motifs at specific memory-associated enhancers with CRISPR base editing or CRISPRi/dCas9 recruitment of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers (e.g., BAF), and ectopically recruit AP-1 to naive loci. Test whether these changes abolish or induce primed accessibility and faster re-induction of the linked gene, which establishes necessity and sufficiency at individual loci.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding, or growth factor), then track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility at defined times after washout, including weeks later. Persistence of AP-1-dependent open regions after the stimulus and AP-1 levels have returned to baseline would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to test maintenance versus initiation
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS, JUN, or the BATF family to remove AP-1 either during priming or after memory is established. Then measure accessibility and the secondary-stimulus transcriptional response. If depletion during priming blocks memory but depletion afterward does not, AP-1 is needed only for initiation. Loss of memory after later depletion would show it is also needed for maintenance.

title: Secondary-challenge response assays (primed versus naive)
description: Compare the RNA-seq and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) response of primed and naive cells to a second stimulus, and relate the strength of the enhanced response to AP-1 motif content at the affected genes. Include dose and time-gap titrations to define how long the memory lasts and whether it is AP-1-dependent.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing across divisions
description: Do paired scRNA/scATAC-seq together with a heritable barcode or clonal tracking in primed cells across several divisions. This tests whether AP-1-associated accessibility states are inherited by daughter cells and whether clonal sister cells share the memory more than random cells do.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and AP-1 site perturbation
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or block specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and use dCas9-based tools to force AP-1 recruitment or histone-mark changes at them without a stimulus. Then check whether accessibility, H3K27ac, and enhanced re-induction are lost or created. This tests whether AP-1 binding at those sites is sufficient and necessary for memory, and whether it works through cooperating factors or chromatin remodelers such as BAF.

title: Persistence after stimulus withdrawal (the song that never stops)
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, serum, or a stress signal) and then withdraw it. Track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq at days to weeks afterward. If AP-1 sites stay open and bound after the signal is gone, that supports AP-1 as a memory mechanism.

title: Sensitivity to the second stimulus (the sweetest tune in the gale)
description: Give a primed and a naive population the same second challenge. Measure the transcriptional response by RNA-seq and nascent-RNA assays, and compare the kinetics and magnitude of induction at AP-1-marked genes. Faster or stronger induction that depends on AP-1 would be the functional signature of memory.

title: Necessity and sufficiency by acute perturbation
description: Use a dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS), degron-tagged JUN/FOS, or CRISPRi of specific enhancers. Apply it either during priming or only during the memory (maintenance) phase, then test whether the memory response is lost. Compare with ectopic AP-1 expression alone to see if it can write memory without the original signal. Separating the establishment and maintenance phases shows whether AP-1 is needed continuously or only to start the memory.

title: Single-cell tracking of AP-1 activity and heritability
description: Use live-cell AP-1 reporters or FOS/JUN imaging, combined with lineage tracing or single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) of sister cells. Test whether the primed state is bistable, is inherited across divisions, and decays with a measurable half-life. Heritability and a stable, all-or-none state would distinguish memory from a simple lingering response.

title: Chromatin mechanism and the independence test
description: Test whether AP-1 maintains memory through chromatin remodeling (BAF/SWI-SNF), histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and pioneer-like opening of closed sites. Perturb these factors after priming, and use optogenetic or inducible AP-1 pulses to ask whether a transient AP-1 input leaves a lasting epigenetic mark. Retained marks that persist when AP-1 is removed would show that the memory is carried by chromatin rather than by continuous AP-1 presence.

title: Trunkless legs: chromatin scars after AP-1 loss
