description: Transiently induce AP-1 (e.g., FOS/JUN pulse or stimulus), then remove it by degron-mediated degradation or dominant-negative A-FOS, and at time points of days to weeks profile ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and CUT&RUN for residual open enhancers. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after the factor is gone, as with the legs that remain after the king, would indicate a memory imprint, and the question is whether it needs continued AP-1 binding.

title: Inscription vs. sand: reversibility and decay kinetics
description: Track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), accessibility and target transcription at repeated time points after the stimulus ends, and fit decay half-lives. Compare them with the cell division number, using synchronized or arrested cells to separate passive dilution from active maintenance, to test whether the memory is stable or erodes like the sand-covered statue.

title: Re-stimulation (primed response) assay
description: Give naive cells and previously stimulated cells (for example, fibroblasts or macrophages after injury or inflammatory exposure) a second stimulus after a rest period, and measure the faster or stronger transcriptional response by RNA-seq or nascent-RNA (PRO-seq). Compare the effect of AP-1 perturbation (CRISPRi on FOS/JUN, or loss of specific enhancers) during the first versus the second exposure to see whether AP-1 is needed to write the memory, to read it, or both.

title: Single-cell lineage-linked memory tracing
description: Use live reporters of AP-1 activity (FOS promoter or AP-1 response element reporters) with barcoded lineage tracing, and record each cell's history of AP-1 activity, then ask whether sister cells inherit similar states and similar future responsiveness. Co-measure single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) to show that AP-1 history predicts the chromatin state better than the current signal does, like a sculptor's reading of a passion that persists in a lifeless thing.

title: Synthetic imprinting by targeted AP-1 recruitment
description: Use dCas9 or a synthetic AP-1 (a tethered or optogenetic JUN/FOS) to bring AP-1 to a chosen locus for a limited time, and then test whether the locus keeps its accessibility and expression after the tool is removed. Compare wild-type motifs with motif mutants and with pioneer or SWI/SNF (BAF) recruitment-deficient variants, to show sufficiency and the mechanism of AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Stipple-map of single-cell AP-1 history (dappled lineage tracing)
description: Use a FOS/JUN knock-in fluorescent or recombinase-based reporter (e.g., Fos-CreER-style tagging) to permanently mark cells that experienced a stimulus, then follow the marked and unmarked 'dappled' mosaic through divisions. Re-challenge and compare transcriptional response and chromatin state between marked and unmarked sister lineages to test whether past AP-1 activity predicts altered future responses.

title: Paired-stimulus priming with washout time course
description: Expose cells to a first AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), wash out, and re-stimulate after variable delays (hours to many cell divisions). Measure the second-response magnitude by RNA-seq and nascent transcription, and test whether AP-1 dose, delay, and motif-linked gene sets quantitatively predict memory duration, using JUN/FOS dominant-negative (A-FOS) to show necessity.

title: Single-cell multiome of AP-1 motif accessibility persistence
description: Run scATAC+RNA-seq before, during, and long after stimulation. Track whether AP-1-motif (chromVAR) accessible regions stay open after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline, and whether this heterogeneity (fast/slow, sweet/sour-like cell states) maps onto subsequent responsiveness at the single-cell level.

title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Tag endogenous AP-1 factors (JUN, FOSL, BATF) with a degron and deplete them either during the priming stimulus or only after the memory state has formed. If memory sites (ChIP/CUT&RUN, ATAC, H3K27ac) persist and the enhanced response remains after AP-1 loss at later times, AP-1 is only an initiator. If memory decays, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

title: Synthetic AP-1 enhancer perturbation and live reporting
description: Use CRISPR dCas9 tools to edit or mutate specific AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers (CRISPRi or base editing), while using live-cell imaging of a reporter at the locus. Test whether the motif is causally needed for faster or stronger reactivation after a prior stimulus, and whether ectopic AP-1 motifs can install memory at a naive locus.

title: Filament-launch time course: transient stimulus then washout with chromatin accessibility profiling
description: Give cells a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA or a cytokine), wash it out, and run ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at several times from hours to weeks. Like the spider's thread that stays in place after launch, this tests whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the signal and AP-1 levels have fallen.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use a dTAG or auxin-inducible degron on JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative A-FOS, applied either during stimulation or after it. If accessibility and transcriptional priming persist when AP-1 is removed after the memory is set, AP-1 is an initiator but not a maintainer. If they collapse, AP-1 is needed continuously, as a thread needs an anchor to hold.

title: Secondary-challenge assay with single-cell multiomics
description: Give a primary stimulus, rest the cells, then give a second stimulus. Use scRNA-seq plus scATAC-seq to compare the faster or stronger gene induction in primed cells against naive cells. Link this to AP-1 motif accessibility and binding at the same loci, and test causality with AP-1 site mutations or CRISPRi at selected enhancers.

title: Live-cell AP-1 dynamics and lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a reporter of AP-1 target activity in single cells across divisions, following lineages after a pulse. Measure how long the state is inherited and whether it is heritable through mitosis, with mitotic bookmarking checked by imaging and mitotic-chromosome ChIP. Each cell sends a filament forward to its daughters, so the tracing asks whether the signal reaches them.

title: Synthetic enhancer-memory reporter and sufficiency test
description: Insert AP-1-motif-only synthetic enhancers driving a reporter into a neutral locus, with motif variants that differ in number, spacing and affinity. Pulse the cells, then measure persistence of reporter activity, accessibility and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at the locus. This tests whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to make a self-sustaining state, and whether it needs cooperating factors or positive feedback loops. Adding an AP-1 recruitment-only control separates binding from a pioneer-like chromatin-remodelling function (BAF recruitment).

title: Decay-kinetics time course of AP-1 chromatin accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Like the 'first green' that fades to ordinary leaf, test whether the early AP-1 state persists or decays: apply a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then run ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and motif-accessibility (chromVAR) at hours, days, and weeks after washout. Persistent AP-1-dependent open sites after signal removal, with measured half-lives, would indicate memory rather than transient response.

title: Primed vs. naive re-stimulation challenge with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then restimulate and compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) to naive cells; repeat with a degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) of FOS/JUN applied only during priming versus only during recall. If AP-1 is needed at priming to produce faster/stronger recall but not at recall, it acts as a memory-writing factor.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory vs. 'subsiding' states
description: Use paired scRNA/scATAC with barcoded lineage tracing to follow clones after a transient stimulus and see whether AP-1 motif accessibility is heritably maintained in daughter cells or reverts to baseline ('leaf subsides to leaf'). Clonal correlation of AP-1 state across divisions, versus random sister-cell divergence, quantifies heritability.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter and imaging of dynamics and bistability
description: Engineer knock-in FOS/JUN fluorescent reporters or AP-1 activity reporters and track single cells with time-lapse microscopy through pulse-and-washout protocols with varied pulse durations and doses. Hysteresis, bimodality, or sustained activity after the stimulus ends suggests a self-sustaining feedback memory; rapid return to baseline suggests none.

title: Ordering test of AP-1 against epigenetic marks with synthetic recruitment
description: At AP-1-dependent loci, map H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and DNA methylation over time after stimulus, and perform motif-mutation CRISPR edits or dCas9-based forced AP-1 recruitment (transient) to ask whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient to establish enhancer marks that outlast its presence. Marks that persist after AP-1 removal indicate AP-1 initiates memory handed off to chromatin, versus AP-1 occupancy itself being the maintained state.

title: Fearful symmetry: paired-daughter lineage tracking of AP-1 state
description: Live-image AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS/JUN endogenous tags plus a TRE-driven reporter) in single cells after a transient stimulus, then compare sister cells across several divisions. Like the tiger's symmetry, high sister-sister correlation that exceeds that of unrelated cells and persists after the stimulus ends would indicate heritable memory rather than ongoing signaling.

title: Seizing the fire: transient pulse then chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy time course
description: Give a defined stimulus pulse (e.g., TPA or a cytokine), wash it out, and run ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS and H3K27ac at days to weeks. Persistent AP-1 motif-enriched accessible sites that stay open after AP-1 levels fall back to baseline indicate that AP-1 left a lasting epigenetic imprint.

title: Burnt fire: acute degron depletion at different times after priming
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-degradable AP-1 subunit (e.g., c-JUN or FOSL1) and remove it either during priming or after it, then restimulate and measure the transcriptional response by RNA-seq. If depletion after priming still leaves the enhanced response, AP-1 is only needed to establish memory. If depletion abolishes the response, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

title: Burning bright in the forest: single-cell multiome of primed vs naive populations
description: Run joint scRNA/scATAC on primed, naive and re-stimulated cells, then infer motif activity with tools like chromVAR and SCENIC. Compare the faster or stronger gene induction at AP-1-dependent loci in primed cells, and test whether the primed subpopulation is a discrete, stable state.

title: What immortal hand: synthetic AP-1 sufficiency test with dCas9 and mutated motifs
description: Delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers by CRISPR, and in parallel tether AP-1 or a pioneer-capable domain to naive loci using dCas9. Loss of memory after motif deletion, and induction of persistent accessibility and heightened response by tethering, would show necessity and sufficiency at specific loci.

title: Transient stimulus, persistent AP-1 chromatin occupancy (the 'deep heart's core' echo)
description: Pulse cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) with a stimulus such as TNF, PMA or wounding, then wash out and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq at days 0, 1, 7 and 21. Like the lake water still heard on grey pavements long after leaving the shore, memory would show up as retained accessible AP-1 motif sites after the stimulus and the FOS/JUN transcripts have decayed.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin-inducible degradation of FOS or JUN (or dominant-negative A-FOS) at different times: before, during, or after the priming stimulus. If AP-1 is only needed during priming but memory persists, it initiates memory. If depleting it after priming erases accessibility and the faster secondary response, it maintains memory.

title: Primed-versus-naive re-stimulation response with motif-site mutagenesis
description: Measure the transcriptional response (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) to a second stimulus in primed and naive cells, and identify the genes with enhanced responses. Then use CRISPR to mutate or dCas9-block the AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers to test whether those sites are necessary for the enhanced response. Add a reporter-based test of whether the primed state is cis-encoded.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability across divisions
description: Track endogenous FOS/JUN with fluorescent knock-in tags and AP-1 reporters in single cells through time, lineage-tracing after stimulus. Test whether state is inherited by daughter cells and decays over a characteristic number of divisions, as expected for epigenetic memory, rather than reflecting continued signaling. Relate the dynamics, such as pulsatile versus sustained, to the memory outcome.

title: Chromatin-state coupling: AP-1 with BAF and histone marks, plus in vivo test
description: Test whether AP-1 recruits BAF remodelers and deposits H3K27ac or H3K4me1 that persist, using BRG1 inhibition, ChIP/CUT&Tag and sequential perturbation. Then check in vivo, for example in skin or after inflammation, whether tissue cells retain AP-1-dependent accessible regions weeks after injury and respond faster on re-challenge.

title: Lone cloud, then crowd: single-cell AP-1 history tracking
description: Live-image endogenous FOS/JUN with knock-in fluorescent reporters (and a stable lineage tracker) in single cells through a first stimulus, a rest period, and a second stimulus. Test whether prior activation history predicts the amplitude or kinetics of the second response, as a wanderer's earlier path predicts where they meet the crowd.

title: Daffodil field mapping: ATAC/CUT&RUN of AP-1 bound latent enhancers
description: Profile AP-1 binding (JUN/FOS CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility and H3K27ac before, after and long after stimulus withdrawal. Identify enhancers that stay open or primed after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and test whether they are the sites that drive faster or stronger reactivation.

title: Breeze-off test: acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells, then use degron-tagged (dTAG/auxin) JUN/FOS or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS to remove AP-1 at defined times: during priming only, during the rest period only, or at restimulation. Compare enhancer accessibility and transcriptional memory to separate AP-1 as the initiator of memory from AP-1 as its maintainer.

title: Dancing in sync: dynamics-encoded memory via optogenetic pulse patterns
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic or chemogenetic input using varied pulse number, frequency and duration, then measure target gene output and chromatin state after a delay. Fit a model, such as a bistable or hysteresis model, to ask whether AP-1 dynamics encode a persistent state that depends on the history of the input.

title: Lineage inheritance across divisions with sister-cell and single-cell multiome
description: Track primed cells through mitosis with time-lapse imaging, or barcode them, then run paired scRNA/scATAC on sisters and distant relatives. Test whether the primed AP-1 target state is inherited, decays at a measurable rate, and is shared more by clonally related cells than by random cells, which would show cell-autonomous heritable memory and not just a persistent external signal.

title: Partial-by-partial 'shaving' of AP-1 subunits with degron tools
description: Like tuning a bell by removing metal from specific partials, acutely degrade individual AP-1 family members (FOS, FOSB, JUN, JUNB, ATF3) with dTAG/auxin degrons after a priming stimulus and measure which ones are needed to maintain versus establish the primed response upon restimulation. Irreversible loss of response after degradation versus recovery after degron washout distinguishes a maintained memory from a transient one.

title: Chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy time course after priming (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN)
description: Prime cells (e.g., with cytokine, wounding signal, or growth factor), then profile accessibility and AP-1 binding at days to weeks after stimulus removal to test whether AP-1-dependent enhancers remain open ('cast' into the chromatin) once AP-1 levels have returned to baseline. Motif-footprint analysis and comparison with naive cells reveal whether AP-1 sites are the persistent memory elements.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage-tracked clonal memory
description: Use barcoded clones and paired scRNA/scATAC to test whether primed AP-1 activity states and target gene responsiveness are inherited across cell divisions in sister cells more than in unrelated cells. Heritability estimates of AP-1 activity and faster re-induction of target genes indicate cell-intrinsic memory rather than persistent signalling.

title: Optogenetic/CRISPR perturbation of AP-1 sites with live reporters
description: Deliver defined pulses of light-controlled AP-1 activation (or dCas9 activation of FOS/JUN) while imaging an AP-1 reporter and endogenous target loci, varying pulse number, duration, and rest interval. A memory mechanism predicts a history-dependent, faster or stronger second response, and mutating specific AP-1 motifs in enhancers by CRISPR tests whether those sites carry the memory.

title: Pioneer-like function and epigenetic mark causality tests
description: Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment) at AP-1 sites after priming, and test whether blocking BAF activity or deacetylation erases memory while forced retention of marks preserves it. Combining this with an in vivo model (e.g., skin inflammatory memory) tests whether AP-1-dependent accessibility is necessary and sufficient for faster secondary responses.

title: Sequence-order decoding of AP-1 dimer history
description: Like a bridge auction where the meaning depends on the order of calls, stimulate cells with ordered pulses (e.g., growth factor then stress, versus the reverse) and measure FOS/JUN/ATF family composition and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for each subunit). Test whether the same stimuli in different orders leave distinct, persistent AP-1 binding and transcriptional states.

title: Pioneer-like priming and persistence of AP-1 sites after stimulus removal
description: Time-course ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and AP-1 CUT&Tag at days to weeks after a transient stimulus, tracking whether AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself returns to baseline. Pair with acute degron depletion (dTAG) of FOS/JUN at different times to determine if AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory or only to establish it.

title: Memory-dependent secondary-response test via AP-1 perturbation
description: Give primed and naive cells a second stimulus and compare faster or stronger induction of target genes (RNA-seq, nascent transcription). Use CRISPRi or mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers, plus dominant-negative A-FOS, to test if the enhanced second response requires those sites.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of AP-1 states
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with heritable barcodes or sister-cell pairs to test whether AP-1 activity states are inherited through cell division. Correlate sister-cell similarity in AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression versus random pairs to quantify heritability beyond shared environment.

title: Decoy-resistance: minimal-signature versus redundant encoding
description: Since a mark that is hard for outside perturbation to disrupt is more useful as memory, challenge primed cells with competing signals, inhibitors of kinases (JNK/ERK) or chromatin writers, and paralog knockouts (e.g., FOSL1/FOSL2 compensation). Measure how robust the memory is and which AP-1 members, cofactors (BAF, p300) or feedback loops stabilize it, using live reporters of an AP-1 target for longitudinal readout.

title: Differential decay of ridge vs. body: component turnover half-lives
description: Like a roof whose ridge wears out far faster than the body, AP-1 memory may persist in some layers (chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs) but decay fast in others (FOS/JUN protein, phosphorylation). Time-course after a transient stimulus measuring FOS/JUN protein and mRNA, JUN phosphorylation, ATAC-seq accessibility at AP-1 motifs, and enhancer H3K27ac, and then fitting decay rates to show which layer carries the memory beyond AP-1 protein levels.

title: Course-by-course ordering: pioneer-like priming by AP-1 in stimulus history
description: Thatch is laid in successive courses where each depends on the one below. Do sequential stimulation (primary then secondary challenge, with variable rest intervals) and use single-cell multiome (scATAC + scRNA) to test whether first-pass AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN/JUNB) opens enhancers that enable faster or larger transcriptional responses to the second stimulus, and whether this is lost when AP-1 is removed.

title: Acute degron removal after the priming stimulus
description: Use dTAG/auxin-degron alleles of FOS, JUN, or dominant-negative A-FOS induced either during priming, or only after priming during the rest period. If memory persists after AP-1 is degraded post-priming, AP-1 is only an initiator. If the memory decays, AP-1 is needed for maintenance. Read out via secondary response magnitude, chromatin accessibility and nascent RNA (PRO-seq).

title: Pitch threshold: dose and duration dependence of memory (bistability)
description: In thatch, the pitch relative to a threshold determines whether the roof sheds water or rots. Test for similar threshold behaviour by titrating stimulus strength and duration, using live-cell AP-1 reporters (FOS-GFP, AP-1 motif reporter) tracked over days in single cells. Look for a bimodal, hysteretic response where cells above a threshold stay ON after stimulus removal, and cells below it return to baseline. Do mathematical modeling of positive feedback (JUN autoregulation) to predict the threshold, then perturb to test it.

title: Locus-specific causal test by motif editing and dCas9 recruitment
description: Like the hazel spars that fix individual bundles, specific AP-1 sites may anchor memory at particular enhancers. Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or recruit dCas9-FOS or dCas9-repressors, and then measure whether the memory of that gene (faster re-induction, retained accessibility, cell-division inheritance across passages) is lost or can be installed ectopically without a stimulus.

title: Transient stimulus, delayed re-challenge (hysteresis test)
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating signal (TPA, TNF, or injury), wash out, then re-stimulate after days to weeks and measure transcriptional response by RNA-seq and nascent-transcript assays. Memory predicts faster or stronger induction of specific genes than in naive cells, and the effect should be lost if c-Jun/c-Fos is knocked out (e.g., degron) only during the first pulse.

title: Case-switching chromatin accessibility: 'upper vs lower case' states
description: Use ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 before, immediately after, and long after stimulus to find enhancers that stay open or primed once AP-1 has left, like type that stays set after the hand moves on. Test causality by showing those enhancers are AP-1 motif-dependent via CRISPR motif mutation or dCas9 perturbation and that persistent accessibility predicts the enhanced re-response.

title: Single-cell tracking of AP-1 dynamics with live reporters
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN (or use a synthetic AP-1 reporter) and image single cells over days to determine whether memory is stored as sustained AP-1 activity, a self-sustaining feedback loop, or as heritable chromatin marks after AP-1 returns to baseline. Correlating prior pulse history with later per-cell response and lineage inheritance across divisions separates cell-autonomous memory from population effects.

title: Acute degron-based necessity and sufficiency with timing control
description: Use inducible degradation of AP-1 (e.g., dTAG on JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS) at different windows: during priming, during the memory interval, and during re-challenge. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, removal during the interval will have no effect, whereas needing it to maintain memory implies ongoing presence; also test sufficiency by transient ectopic expression of AP-1 in naive cells.

title: Tightness metric: dose-dependence and decay kinetics of memory
description: Quantify how memory scales with pulse strength, duration and number of repeats, and measure its half-life and persistence across cell divisions, forming a quantitative model (e.g., bistable vs graded) of how much 'spacing' is needed to lock the state. Fit the data with a dynamical model and verify its predictions, such as bistability with a threshold, by sorting cells and checking for bimodal, heritable states.

title: Slip-style sequential occupancy mapping of AP-1 co-binding
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or a stress signal), profile FOS/JUN family members, the pioneer partner, and chromatin accessibility (CUT&RUN/ATAC) over days to weeks. The aim is to see whether AP-1 'signatories' accumulate on the same enhancers and whether the lead factor's early binding predicts later accessibility and H3K27ac, as in a slip where followers join the lead underwriter. Persistence of sites after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Acute degron depletion at defined times after stimulus
description: Use dTAG/AID degrons on c-Jun, c-Fos, or JunB to remove AP-1 either during the stimulus or after it has ended, then measure the primed transcriptional response to a second stimulus. If memory requires AP-1 only at induction, the enhancer state persists after removal. If it requires AP-1 continuously, the memory collapses once AP-1 is removed. This separates AP-1 as the writer of memory from AP-1 as the carrier of memory.

title: Single-cell paired readout of AP-1 dynamics and re-stimulation response
description: Combine live-cell reporters for FOS/JUN activity (or a knock-in fluorescent tag) with a prime–rest–restimulate protocol, followed by single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC). Test whether the history of AP-1 activity in each cell, such as its amplitude and duration, predicts that cell's secondary response, and whether the memory is binary across cells (like the all-at-once bell signal) or graded.

title: Enhancer-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 motifs
description: Use CRISPR base editing or saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, together with dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-based eviction, applied before or after priming. Measure whether the motif is required for establishing the open state, for keeping it, and for faster re-induction of the linked gene. Compare with other motifs to show that the memory is attributable to AP-1 sites specifically.

title: Memory kinetics and heritability across cell divisions
description: Track primed chromatin state (accessibility, histone marks, nascent transcription by PRO-seq) in lineages after stimulus washout, with time-lapse lineage tracing or sorted daughter cells across multiple divisions. Fit decay models and test whether AP-1-dependent states are inherited through mitosis (by mitotic-chromatin CUT&RUN for AP-1 bookmarking) or are rebuilt each cycle. Compare half-lives with and without AP-1 perturbation to quantify its contribution to memory.

title: Trimmed-consensus scoring of AP-1 occupancy across independent assays
description: Like discarding the highest and lowest judges, profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and accessibility after a transient stimulus using several independent assays (CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq with different antibodies, footprinting) and labs/replicates. Drop the extreme scores per locus and average the rest, so that only sites with robust, reproducible persistence long after the stimulus is gone are called memory sites, not artifacts of one antibody or batch.

title: Base value vs. execution: separating priming potential from realized response
description: For each AP-1-bound enhancer, define a fixed 'base value' (motif strength, prior accessibility, baseline binding) and a separate 'execution grade' (transcriptional output, e.g., nascent RNA/PRO-seq, upon re-stimulation). Model whether prior exposure increases execution beyond what the base value predicts, to test if AP-1 history adds information beyond sequence and chromatin state.

title: Completed-rotation test: acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus ends
description: Like the technical panel checking whether a rotation was fully completed, test whether memory is fully established and maintained without ongoing AP-1. Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS added at defined times (during priming, after priming, before restimulation) and measure whether accessibility and faster re-induction are lost, to distinguish AP-1 as initiator versus maintainer of memory.

title: Quarter-turn sensitivity: motif mutation and dose-titration at single enhancers
description: Small deviations can cost a lot, so make precise perturbations: CRISPR base-editing of single AP-1 motifs (partial vs. full disruption) and titration of stimulus dose/duration. Measure the effect on persistent accessibility and re-stimulation response to find threshold-like (nonlinear) behavior, indicating AP-1 sites as discrete memory switches.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of memory inheritance through division
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with lineage barcodes or sister-cell pairing after transient stimulation, and live imaging of AP-1 reporters or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN. Test whether primed AP-1 target states are inherited by daughter cells and correlate with AP-1 binding retained through mitosis (mitotic bookmarking), compared with unstimulated controls.

title: Angled-tesserae: single-cell ATAC/CUT&Tag of AP-1 motif accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., epithelial or immune cells with a wound/inflammatory cue), remove the stimulus, and track at single-cell resolution which AP-1 (FOS/JUN) motif-bearing enhancers stay open for days to weeks. Like tesserae whose tilt persists after the candle moves, persistent accessibility at specific sites, heterogeneous between cells, would indicate stored state; compare to unstimulated and to cells re-challenged later.

title: Re-stimulation 'flicker' test of primed response
description: Give a first pulse of stimulus, rest for variable intervals, then a second pulse, and measure transcription (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) and AP-1 binding kinetics versus naive cells. Faster or stronger induction at AP-1-dependent genes that decays with rest time quantifies memory duration; the response varying with 'viewing angle' (pulse timing, dose) maps the memory's dependence on history.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment, maintenance, and recall
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 factors, depleting them before the first stimulus, during the rest period, or only at re-challenge. If depletion only at establishment erases memory while depletion during the rest period doesn't, AP-1 initiates but doesn't maintain it; loss at maintenance or recall shows AP-1 is itself the memory carrier.

title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1 motifs at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or motif deletion at individual AP-1 sites, plus dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers (e.g., BAF), to test whether single sites are necessary and sufficient for retained accessibility and faster re-induction. Following the 'outline row' idea, a few key boundary sites guiding the larger pattern should show disproportionate effects, which can be tested by ranking sites by effect size.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 dynamics and lineage-tracked memory
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN (and a reporter of target genes) in single cells across stimulation, rest, and re-stimulation, tracking cell lineages through division. Correlating a mother cell's AP-1 history with daughters' reporter responses tests heritability, and resolution depends on 'viewing distance': single-cell traces look noisy but population-level patterns resolve into distinct memory states.

title: Stimulus-washout chromatin accessibility time course
description: Expose cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts) to a transient stimulus such as TNF, LPS, or wounding cues, then wash out and profile ATAC-seq, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN and H3K27ac at multiple timepoints out to weeks. Persistent AP-1-motif-containing accessible sites after AP-1 binding itself has decayed would indicate a memory that outlasts the signal; this is analogous to a crease that stays after the paper is unfolded.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined windows (induction vs maintenance)
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 components to remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only after washout, then restimulate and measure transcriptional response by RNA-seq and accessibility. If depletion during the priming phase prevents memory but depletion in the maintenance phase does not, AP-1 acts as an initiator; the converse implies it actively maintains the memory.

title: Vertex-style combinatorial constraint analysis of AP-1 motif grammar
description: Map memory-associated enhancers and quantify AP-1 motif number, spacing, orientation, and co-occurrence with partner TFs (e.g., ETS, CEBP, NFAT) using massively parallel reporter assays with systematically varied motif arrangements. Like flat-fold rules that require angle sums and fold counts to balance at each vertex, this tests whether specific rules of motif combination predict which sites retain memory and which return to baseline.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage-tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA plus ATAC with barcode lineage tracing or sister-cell pairing after stimulation to test whether AP-1 activity states and accessibility are shared among sister cells across divisions more than expected by chance. High sister concordance that persists for generations, and that predicts the magnitude of secondary response, would support heritable memory rather than transient signaling.

title: Targeted epigenome editing of AP-1-dependent memory loci
description: Use dCas9-based tools (CRISPRi/KRAB, or motif mutation by base editing) at individual AP-1-bound enhancers that stay open after stimulation, and test the effect on faster or stronger reinduction of the nearby gene. Packing analogy: each enhancer is a circle that must be placed individually, so loci-specific perturbation shows which sites are necessary and sufficient, and whether the memory is cis-encoded or depends on global AP-1 levels.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing of AP-1 state
description: The material looks like a series of short, distinct random tokens, which suggests using unique heritable barcodes. Barcode individual cells, give a transient AP-1 stimulus, and use single-cell RNA-seq with an AP-1 target signature to test whether sister cells share AP-1 activity states after washout more than unrelated cells do. Shared states across divisions would indicate heritable memory.

title: Scrambled-motif enhancer editing
description: In the material, scrambling the characters destroys the message while the overall composition stays the same. Likewise, use CRISPR to scramble or delete AP-1 (TRE) motifs at candidate enhancers while leaving the surrounding sequence intact. Then test whether those enhancers lose primed accessibility and faster re-induction, which would show that the AP-1 motif itself carries the memory.

title: Optogenetic pulse-history encoding
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemogenetic control using different pulse patterns (single long, several short, and spaced pulses) that deliver the same total dose. Measure later target gene output to see whether the response depends on the stimulus history and not only on the current AP-1 level. History-dependent output is a functional signature of memory.

title: Time-resolved chromatin profiling after washout
description: After a transient stimulus, collect ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag data (FOS/JUN, H3K27ac) at several time points, from hours to multiple cell divisions. Identify sites that keep their accessibility or occupancy after AP-1 protein returns to baseline, and test whether the persistence predicts stronger re-induction of nearby genes.

title: Hysteresis and maintenance test by acute depletion
description: Ramp the stimulus dose up and then down and look for hysteresis, which indicates bistability. In parallel, use an inducible degron on AP-1 factors during the priming phase or only during the later memory phase. If depletion in the memory phase does not erase the primed response, AP-1 is needed for establishing memory but not for maintaining it. If it does erase the response, AP-1 is needed for maintenance.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (hysteresis test)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or stress) that activates AP-1 (Fos/Jun), let activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate after varying intervals and measure target gene transcription and AP-1 occupancy. Faster or stronger secondary responses that depend on the first exposure would indicate memory, as would a decay time constant longer than the half-lives of the Fos/Jun proteins. Like the material's random token stream, where only a pattern recurring across the sequence counts as signal, a response counts as memory only if it recurs in a history-dependent way and isn't a one-off burst.

title: Chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting over time
description: Run ATAC-seq or CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, along with H3K27ac and H3K4me1, before, during and long after stimulation. Look for AP-1-dependent enhancers that stay open or primed after AP-1 levels have fallen, which would show the stimulus left a lasting chromatin mark. Motif-level footprinting across the time course can separate persistent occupancy from persistent accessibility.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 after the priming phase
description: Use a degron (dTAG/auxin) or a dominant-negative such as A-Fos to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after it, then test whether the primed state persists. If the memory survives AP-1 loss after priming, AP-1 acts as an initiator that sets epigenetic marks. If the memory is lost, AP-1 is needed continuously to maintain it. Comparing the two timings separates these two mechanisms.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporters
description: Track endogenously tagged c-Fos/c-Jun or an AP-1 reporter in single cells across repeated stimulations to see whether activity states are heritable through division. Compare sister-cell correlation and lineage trees against shuffled controls to find whether the response states are inherited, as would be expected for memory, or arise from independent noise.

title: Motif mutation and synthetic enhancer test of sufficiency
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and separately insert a synthetic AP-1 site at a neutral locus, then measure whether transient AP-1 signalling is enough to produce lasting accessibility and primed transcription. Mutating the motif shows whether it is necessary, and the synthetic insert shows whether it is sufficient to encode the memory.

title: Random-string scrambling control for memory readout
description: Like the material, which is a random character string with no recoverable signal, build a null model by shuffling AP-1 motif positions and ChIP/ATAC labels across the genome. Compare real persistence of AP-1 binding after stimulus withdrawal against this shuffled null to show that retained accessibility is not chance.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal time-course of AP-1 occupancy and accessibility
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient stimulus, remove it, and track CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN plus ATAC-seq at days 0 to 14. Sites that stay open and AP-1 bound long after FOS/JUN transcript levels return to baseline indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming vs. before
description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS (dTAG) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during rechallenge. If memory persists when AP-1 is removed after priming, it's held by other factors. If it is lost, AP-1 maintains the memory.

title: Secondary stimulation response with motif mutation
description: Use CRISPR editing or dCas9 interference to mutate AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, then measure the enhanced transcriptional response to a second stimulus by RNA-seq or reporter assays. This tests whether specific sites are necessary for faster, stronger re-induction.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Perform paired scRNA/ATAC on clonally related sister cells after priming and several divisions. Test whether AP-1-linked accessibility is inherited more similarly within clones than across them, and whether it predicts each cell's rechallenge response.

title: Chromatin accessibility memory after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TPA, growth factor, or injury signal), then wash out and perform ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at time points over days to weeks. Persistent AP-1 motif-containing accessible sites after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate a retained memory state. Like the material's string of random-looking characters, the sites that persist are a sparse signal that must be separated from noise by comparing against unstimulated controls and shuffled-motif backgrounds.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin-inducible degron tagging of FOS or JUN (or a dominant-negative A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the stimulus or only after memory is established. If accessibility and the enhanced secondary response persist after depletion post-establishment, AP-1 is needed only for writing the memory. If they collapse, AP-1 is needed for maintaining it.

title: Re-stimulation response assay (primed vs naive)
description: Give a first stimulus, rest the cells, then give a second stimulus. Compare RNA-seq and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) between primed and naive cells, and check whether the faster or stronger induction is limited to AP-1-bound loci. Include a no-first-stimulus control and a first-stimulus-with-AP-1-inhibition control to show the dependence.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Do single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling, with barcodes or live reporter imaging to identify sister cells, after a transient stimulus and several divisions. Test whether sister cells share AP-1 site accessibility and responsiveness more than random pairs, which would indicate mitotic inheritance. Live-cell AP-1 reporters can also show whether the memory is bistable or graded.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 perturbation and histone context
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment or an inducible pulse of AP-1 at a defined enhancer, and measure whether it creates lasting accessibility and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 after the trigger is removed. Pair this with perturbation of cofactors such as BAF/SWI-SNF, and with motif mutation by CRISPR base editing. This tests whether AP-1 alone is sufficient and which co-factors stabilize the memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed ATAC/CUT&Tag readout
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA or inflammatory cue) and then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding by ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag after a long washout. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after the signal and AP-1 activity have returned to baseline would indicate a memory-like chromatin state. Like the material's string of short, mostly non-repeating tokens, this relies on individually unique 'marks' being retained after the signal ends.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use a dTAG/auxin degron on JUN/FOS, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, at defined times: during the priming stimulus, or only during the washout. Then test whether the primed enhanced re-response is lost. Loss when AP-1 is removed only during the washout shows ongoing AP-1 is needed to maintain memory; loss only when removed during priming shows it acts as an initiator.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporter history
description: Image AP-1 activity with a live reporter or a FOS/JUN biosensor across repeated stimulation pulses in single cells, then relate each cell's prior pulse history to its later response amplitude. Cell-to-cell heterogeneity and the persistence of individual cells' response states over days and divisions would distinguish true memory from continued signaling.

title: Synthetic AP-1 site perturbation at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs or tether dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-p300 at specific primed enhancers, and measure re-stimulation transcription (RNA-seq/PRO-seq) and H3K27ac. If memory-linked genes lose faster or stronger secondary responses only when their AP-1 motifs are disrupted, this shows AP-1 binding is causal rather than merely correlated.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and inheritance assay
description: Synchronize and sort primed cells, and map FOS/JUN occupancy on mitotic chromosomes by CUT&RUN. Follow lineage-tracked daughter cells through several divisions, measuring whether enhanced responsiveness and AP-1-associated accessibility are inherited. Retained AP-1 binding on mitotic chromatin and transmission of primed responses to daughter cells would support heritable memory.

title: Scrambled-token chromatin priming time course
description: The material is a string of random 5–7 character tokens, each unique and order-independent. Treat each stimulus as a distinct token and expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or injury). Then use ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN over days to weeks to see whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the stimulus is gone. A second challenge then tests for faster or stronger transcription at those sites.

title: Combinatorial dimer-code perturbation
description: The material resembles a code built from many different token combinations, so the idea is that AP-1 memory may be encoded in which FOS/JUN/ATF dimers form, not just in total AP-1 activity. Use dimer-specific CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq, plus targeted degradation of individual members (dTAG), to find which compositions at which enhancers are needed to maintain primed states.

title: Single-cell lineage-barcoded heterogeneity test
description: Each token is unique, like a cell barcode. Label clonal lineages with barcodes, stimulate transiently, and use single-cell multiome (RNA plus ATAC) to ask whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility and response strength after division more than random cells do. Shared states would indicate heritable memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells, then remove AP-1 (inducible degron or dominant-negative A-FOS) after the stimulus ends and before re-challenge. If memory needs continuous AP-1, the primed accessibility and enhanced response should decay. If AP-1 only initiates memory, they should persist. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Synthetic AP-1 reporter with live imaging
description: Build a reporter with AP-1 motifs in varied arrangements and spacings, like arranging tokens in different sequences. Image single cells over multiple stimulus pulses with varied intervals to quantify hysteresis, pulse-history dependence, and decay time. Mutating motifs or adding methylation inhibitors tests which sequence features and chromatin marks carry the memory.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed ATAC/CUT&RUN re-challenge
description: Expose cells to a defined stimulus (e.g., TPA or serum), wash out, and let AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels return to baseline. Then map chromatin accessibility and AP-1 binding (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN) days later and compare transcriptional responses to a second challenge with naive cells. Like the scrambled material, where the characters carry no obvious order until a key is applied, the 'memory' should only show up when the second stimulus decodes the retained chromatin state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use a degron (dTAG/auxin) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 at different times: during the initial stimulus only, or only after washout. If primed accessibility and the faster re-response persist after AP-1 is gone, AP-1 acts as an initiator. If they are lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory. Comparing the two outcomes separates the two roles.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of priming and heterogeneity
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq across stimulus, washout and re-stimulation time points. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility in individual cells predicts the strength of the later response and whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells. Lineage barcoding or cell-division tracking would link inheritance to memory rather than to persistent signaling.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and target loci
description: Image fluorescently tagged FOS/JUN together with a transcriptional reporter of an AP-1 target gene through repeated pulses. Quantify whether previous pulses change the amplitude, timing or probability of later responses, and whether this lasts across divisions. Fitting the data with mathematical models of hysteresis or bistability would distinguish a true memory (history-dependent, self-sustaining) from slow decay of the signal.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and histone-mark profiling at AP-1 sites
description: Profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and nucleosome remodeling (BAF/SWI-SNF) at AP-1-bound enhancers after the first stimulus and after washout. Then use dCas9-based editing to erase or install these marks, or to mutate AP-1 motifs, at selected enhancers and test for causal gain or loss of primed re-responses. This links AP-1 binding to a persistent chromatin state at specific loci.

title: Random-string "tokens" as barcoded stimulation history
description: The material is a series of short random tokens of varying length and character composition. Treat it as an analogy for barcoding: give cells a brief, distinct AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., anisomycin, TPA, or EGF) and record each cell's history with a heritable lineage barcode or fluorescent reporter. After a washout of days to weeks, test whether the original stimulus can be read out from chromatin accessibility (scATAC) and from the transcriptional response to a second challenge.

title: Priming and re-stimulation memory assay with ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq
description: Stimulate cells once, wash out, rest them for several cell cycles, then re-stimulate. Compare the transcriptional kinetics and magnitude of the second response with those of naive cells (RNA-seq, nascent RNA). Map the retained AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and accessibility at enhancers with ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN, and test whether the sites that stay open predict which genes respond faster.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times (dTAG/AID)
description: Use degron-tagged FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 at set times after the initial stimulus. Removal after the stimulus ends but before re-challenge tests whether AP-1 itself must persist to maintain memory, or whether it is only needed to establish it. Measure whether accessibility and the enhanced second response persist without AP-1.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Image FOS/JUN reporters or endogenously tagged proteins in lineages over several divisions, using microfluidic pulse protocols that vary pulse number, duration and spacing. Quantify whether the dynamics of a mother cell predict those of its daughters, and whether the second-response amplitude depends on the pattern of earlier pulses, which would suggest a history-dependent state rather than a transient one.

title: Pioneer-like activity and chromatin-mark causality tests
description: Check whether AP-1 recruits chromatin remodelers (BAF) and deposits H3K27ac or H3K4me1 at memory enhancers, and whether those marks persist after AP-1 is gone. Use dCas9-based epigenome editing to add or remove the marks at specific enhancers, or use an AP-1 motif mutation, and measure the effect on memory of the response. This separates AP-1 as the mark-writing trigger from the chromatin state as the carrier of memory.

title: Pheromone-evaporation test: AP-1 decay kinetics vs. memory persistence
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding, or cytokine pulse), measure the half-lives of AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN/ChIP time course, live-cell FOS/JUN reporters) and of the chromatin accessibility it created (ATAC-seq), then use acute degron removal (dTAG on FOS/JUN) at varied delays to test whether the memory is held by AP-1 itself or persists once it is gone. Memory that requires continuous AP-1 behaves like a trail needing constant renewal, whereas memory that persists after AP-1 removal is self-sustaining. The 'forgetting' rate is then compared with the rate at which re-stimulation response is lost.

title: Desiccation-and-rewatering primed-response assay with single-cell multiome
description: Give cells a first stimulus, let them return to baseline for days (the 'dry' phase), then deliver a second stimulus and measure the primed response by scRNA+ATAC multiome, comparing naive, primed, and AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) or degron-treated cells. Test whether the faster or stronger second response depends on AP-1 sites that stayed open as 'latent' accessible elements, and whether the dependence is cell-autonomous by tracking lineages via barcodes across division.

title: Moiré combinatorics: dimer-composition code across two input grids
description: AP-1 dimers (FOS/JUN/ATF/MAF families) combine with partner TFs (e.g., ETS, NFAT, lineage TFs) to produce composite motifs. Use paired perturbation of dimer composition and partner presence (CRISPRi/degron matrix) with ChIP/CUT&Tag and MPRA to test whether history is encoded in which dimer and partner pairs were engaged — a pattern neither input contains alone. Predict that a history-specific dimer/partner signature at enhancers can decode a cell's past stimulus from chromatin state with a classifier trained on known histories.

title: Kintsugi of a flawed reporter: using imperfect AP-1 sites as memory switches
description: Use CRISPR base-editing or saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at a memory-associated enhancer to create variants with weakened (flawed) affinity, then test whether the suboptimal sites are the ones that retain memory, e.g., by sustaining accessibility with slow decay, while consensus TRE sites respond quickly and forget. Quantify with MPRA and locus-specific live imaging (dCas9 or reporter) across stimulus histories. This asks whether imperfection in motif affinity is what gives hysteresis, like a bell flaw setting its pitch.

title: Sandpile-style dose-history mapping: same factor, different causes
description: Apply stimuli of different types (mechanical, inflammatory, growth factor, injury) with systematically varied intensity, duration, and spacing, and measure induced AP-1 composition, enhancer occupancy, and downstream gene state with time-resolved CUT&Tag and RNA-seq. Fit a dynamical (bistability/hysteresis) model to ask whether AP-1 'avalanche' responses show threshold, history-dependent state transitions, and avalanche-size distributions that differ by stimulus cause even though the same factor is activated. Validate by predicting the outcome of untested stimulus sequences.

title: Rope-fiber test: relay of AP-1 occupancy across short-lived members
description: Rope strength comes from overlapping fibers, none of which spans the whole length. Test whether memory persists even though no single AP-1 protein or complex persists: use degron-tagged FOS/JUN family members, pulse-label with HaloTag, and run CUT&Tag at timepoints long after a stimulus. If sites stay occupied while the original molecules have turned over, memory is carried by a relay of exchanging subunits and chromatin state. If occupancy requires the original molecules, it is not.

title: Salt-ring chromatin accessibility record of past stimuli
description: Each drought leaves its own ring, so the crust is a stack of records. Stimulate cells with repeated, distinct pulses (e.g., TPA, then anisomycin, then serum) and run single-cell ATAC plus AP-1 motif-resolved footprinting. Test whether each stimulus leaves a separable, ordered accessibility signature at AP-1 sites that persists after washout and reads out history. Dropping FOS or JUN acutely, or placing a dominant-negative (A-FOS) after the stimulus, tests whether AP-1 is needed to maintain the record rather than only to write it.

title: Noise as ingredient: single-cell AP-1 fluctuation spectra predict memory
description: Treat transcriptional noise as the signal. Live-image an endogenous FOS/JUN reporter (MS2 or knock-in fluorescent tag) in single cells over days and measure the autocorrelation and pulse statistics of AP-1 activity. Test whether cells with higher pulse frequency or longer autocorrelation retain a primed response (faster, stronger re-induction of target genes) on restimulation. Then use optogenetic control of pulse patterns, with the same total dose delivered as bursts or as a plateau, to causally test whether the temporal pattern encodes memory.

title: Kintsugi perturbation: break AP-1 sites and see whether the scar becomes the memory
description: The fracture becomes the most valuable line. Use CRISPR to damage individual AP-1 motifs at enhancers, or use CRISPRi/dCas9 to evict AP-1 transiently, in cells with primed enhancers. Then quantify whether repair or recovery leaves a stable epigenetic scar, such as altered H3K27ac, methylation, or reduced re-binding, and whether the response to a second stimulus is changed. Comparing wild-type with a mutated motif and with transient eviction separates sequence-encoded memory from state-encoded memory.

title: Lichen test: AP-1 and a partner as a joint memory unit
description: Two organisms filing one return suggests that memory belongs to the pair and not to either partner. Test whether AP-1 memory needs a partner such as a pioneer factor (e.g., ETS, CEBP, or SWI/SNF/BAF). Acutely degrade AP-1 or the partner after priming, and use sequential ChIP or CUT&RUN co-occupancy plus Micro-C to map the joint state. Memory that is lost only when both are present, or only when the partner is removed, would show that AP-1 recruits a memory-bearing complex and does not itself store it.

title: Bell-lip tuning: perturb enhancer edges, not the AP-1 core
description: Instead of knocking out AP-1 (the crown), use CRISPR base editing or dCas9 to subtly alter AP-1 motif flanks, spacing, and affinity at the lip of primed enhancers, then quantify how the strength and duration of a stimulus-induced memory response (accessibility via ATAC, transcriptional re-induction kinetics) shift. A graded, tunable dose-response of memory to motif affinity would show AP-1 sequence encodes memory rather than just being required for activation.

title: Negative-space footprinting of AP-1 after it leaves
description: After transient stimulation (e.g., TPA, wounding signal, or inflammatory cue) and AP-1 washout, use CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors alongside ATAC footprinting, histone marks (H3K4me1, H3K27ac) and the SWI/SNF (BAF) complex to map the 'key-shaped hole': accessible, BAF-marked sites that retain open chromatin once AP-1 is gone. Compare days to weeks later and with acute AP-1 degradation (dTAG/auxin degron) to test whether the memory persists independent of continued AP-1 binding or needs it to be maintained.

title: Trehalose-style dormancy: AP-1 memory across quiescence and division
description: Prime cells, then push them into quiescence (serum starvation or contact inhibition) or through multiple cell cycles, holding for days to weeks with no AP-1 activity (monitored by live AP-1 reporters). Re-challenge and test whether primed loci retain the faster, stronger response and whether mitotic bookmarking by AP-1 (live-cell imaging, mitotic-chromosome ChIP) explains persistence, with degron removal of AP-1 during dormancy as the causal control.

title: Single-cell lineage-traced memory with un-averaged readouts
description: Combine barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome (scRNA + scATAC) to compare sister cells after a primary stimulus and re-stimulus, testing whether the response of a sister predicts the other's response beyond what shared AP-1 dynamics predict. Heritable, clone-specific, bimodal memory states that track with AP-1-dependent accessibility would be invisible in bulk averages and would distinguish true cellular memory from persistent signaling.

title: Slime-mold rewiring: optogenetic AP-1 pulse-pattern training
description: Use optogenetic control of AP-1 (e.g., light-inducible c-Fos/c-Jun or upstream kinases) to deliver defined pulse trains of varying frequency, duration and spacing, then measure whether later responses depend on the history of the pattern, like a network re-routing its paths after use. Pair with live reporters of target genes and ATAC to build a history-to-state map and test for hallmarks of memory: dependence on training pattern, spacing effects, decay time, and erasure by counter-stimuli.

title: Shake-to-ratchet: noisy re-stimulation reveals hysteresis
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding cytokines, or optogenetic FOS/JUN), then apply a second stimulus of varying strength and timing, with and without deliberately injected noise (pulsed or fluctuating dosing). Measure AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC) and target transcription. Memory predicts a primed-vs-naive hysteresis loop in the dose-response, and noise should reveal whether the ratchet advances only under fluctuation.

title: Dead-layer-carries-the-living: AP-1-opened enhancer residue after AP-1 loss
description: After priming, remove AP-1 with an acute degron on FOS/JUN, or a dominant-negative A-FOS, at several delays. Track by time-resolved ATAC, H3K27ac and H3K4me1 whether the accessible 'scar' persists and whether it accelerates re-induction of genes upon AP-1 return. If the scaffold persists without AP-1 and drives faster recall, AP-1 acts as a writer of memory, not just a carrier.

title: Silence as measurement: single-cell live reporters of AP-1 dynamics across divisions
description: Use live-cell reporters of endogenous FOS/JUN activity and a target gene in lineage-tracked single cells. Measure whether past AP-1 pulse history in a mother cell predicts response amplitude in daughters, and compute mutual information between history and response across generations. Cells that stay quiet in between are informative controls, since memory without ongoing AP-1 activity argues for a non-AP-1-bound carrier.

title: Pioneer-site occupancy swap: AP-1 binding-site editing and dCas9 tethering
description: Mutate or CRISPRi/CRISPRa individual AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, and tether synthetic AP-1 or chromatin-remodeler recruiters at the same loci. Then test whether a site is necessary and sufficient to confer faster, stronger secondary responses, which separates local enhancer memory from global cell-state memory.

title: Slime-mold rewiring: perturb-and-recover network reconstruction
description: Perform Perturb-seq or multiome sequencing on cells at different times after a transient AP-1 stimulus, delete AP-1 family members (FOS, JUN, ATF, MAF) and ask how the regulatory network (TF-to-enhancer-to-gene links) reroutes. Compare rebuilt networks to the original and to naive cells, and quantify path-dependence. Stable differences after wash-out would indicate that AP-1 has set a persistent network state.

title: Kintsugi chromatin: engineered AP-1 site breaks as load-bearing
description: Use CRISPR to disrupt individual AP-1 motifs in enhancers that gained accessibility after a transient stimulus (e.g., FOS/JUN induction or injury), then repair or rescue them with synthetic motifs at shifted positions. Measure whether the fracture and rescue site become the persistent accessibility/H3K27ac anchor after the stimulus ends, via ATAC-seq and re-stimulation response magnitude weeks later.

title: Loser-pays dose titration: cost of memory vs. dynamics of AP-1 pulses
description: Deliver defined AP-1 activation pulses (optogenetic FOS/JUN or c-Jun degron systems) varying duration, amplitude and frequency, then wash out. Quantify the 'price' paid in retained accessibility and faster transcriptional re-induction on secondary challenge, to test whether memory requires a threshold of AP-1 dwell time rather than simple presence.

title: Mycelial-delay test: AP-1 occupancy decay versus chromatin persistence
description: After a stimulus, time-resolve AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS) alongside accessibility, histone marks and nascent transcription over days to weeks and through cell divisions. If AP-1 leaves while accessibility persists, it acts as a pioneer 'initiator'. If its presence is required, acute degradation (dTAG) at various delays after stimulus should erase memory only within a defined window, so the delay itself is the measurement.

title: Comparison-only apprentice: paired lineage-matched memory vs. naive cells without absolute quantification
description: Use single-cell multiome (ATAC+RNA) on matched primed vs. naive clones or lineage-barcoded sister cells, and rank-compare AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) and target gene responsiveness only within pairs. Test whether sister-cell pairs inherit the same relative AP-1 state across divisions, giving a heritability estimate of the memory independent of batch or absolute signal.

title: Moiré interference: AP-1 combined with a second factor's grid
description: Map composite motifs (AP-1 plus ETS, NFAT, or glucocorticoid receptor) genome-wide and test with MPRA and genomic perturbations whether memory loci are specifically ones where AP-1 partners with a cell-type factor, since the emergent pattern would exceed either factor alone. Knock out each partner separately and together to see if retained accessibility requires the combination.

title: Tidal-pool pulsing: AP-1 dynamics tuned to stimulus schedule
description: Expose cells to AP-1-activating stimuli (e.g., TPA, anisomycin, optogenetic c-Fos/JUN) in periodic regimes with varied period and duty cycle, then measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target-gene response to a later test challenge. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, the priming should depend on the schedule (frequency tuning) and not just on total dose, and should outlast AP-1 protein levels.

title: Keyhole/negative-space footprinting of AP-1 sites after stimulus withdrawal
description: After transient stimulation, track time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag with TF footprinting to find AP-1 motif sites that stay open after AP-1 occupancy is lost, i.e., the 'keyhole' left behind. Compare with H3K27ac/H3K4me1 and with sites in cells never stimulated to test whether the accessible state persists and carries memory without ongoing AP-1 binding.

title: Acute degradation as the decisive intervention (dTAG/auxin degron of FOS/JUN)
description: Use degron-tagged FOS or JUN (or dominant-negative A-FOS) to remove AP-1 at defined stages: before the priming stimulus (is it needed to establish memory?), during the resting interval (is it needed to maintain memory?), and at re-stimulation (is it needed to read it out?). Readouts are RNA-seq and accessibility on re-challenge, separating establishment, maintenance and recall roles.

title: Self-repelling trail: single-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 history
description: Use a live reporter of AP-1 activity, such as a destabilized and a stable fluorescent reporter pair or a Cre-based recorder that permanently marks past AP-1 activation, combined with lineage tracing and later re-stimulation. Test whether cells and daughters with a recorded history respond more strongly or faster, and for how many divisions, which separates cell-autonomous heritable memory from ongoing signaling.

title: Bell-tuning by edits: mutate AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or enhancer-deletion screens (MPRA plus endogenous editing) to alter AP-1 motif number, spacing and affinity at loci that show primed responses. Measure how these changes shift the strength and duration of the memory phenotype, to show whether AP-1 sites are necessary and sufficient, and whether the 'flaws' in motif quality tune the memory decay.

title: Craquelure-style chromatin fracture mapping after transient stimulus
description: Shard mechanism (lacquer craquelure): the pattern of failure records the history of the underlying shrinkage. After a transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), later perturb the system with a stressor (AP-1 degron depletion, BAF inhibition) and map which enhancers lose accessibility (ATAC/CUT&Tag) and in what order. Compare the loss pattern between naive and previously stimulated cells to test whether the 'fracture' map encodes the history of earlier AP-1 exposure.

title: Losing-bid analysis: sites AP-1 binds but fails to open
description: Shard mechanism (auction losing bids carry information): the rejected options reveal the decision rules. Use time-resolved ChIP/CUT&RUN plus ATAC across repeated stimulations to catalog AP-1 motif sites that are bound transiently but never become accessible or never retain accessibility. Compare their sequence, nucleosome, and cofactor features with sites that are retained to define the rules for which AP-1 binding is converted into memory and which is not.

title: Moiré interference between two stimulus rhythms
description: Shard mechanism (moiré arises only when two regular grids are slightly misaligned): a slow beat pattern emerges from a small mismatch of periodic inputs. Deliver optogenetic or chemical AP-1 pulses at two slightly offset periods or in two pathways (e.g., JNK and ERK), then measure whether the residual enhancer accessibility and gene expression show a slow beat or phase-dependent memory. The aim is to test whether AP-1 integrates stimulus timing rather than just dose, and to distinguish dynamics-based memory from a simple ratchet.

title: Subtractive tuning: shave AP-1 dosage to find the memory-critical threshold
description: Shard mechanism (bell founders tune by removing metal, not adding): precision comes from graded subtraction of an existing structure. Instead of overexpression, use titratable degrons (dTAG/AID) or CRISPRi alleles of FOS/JUN family members and motif-site edits to remove AP-1 stepwise at defined times (during priming, during the delay, or during recall). Measure how recall amplitude and chromatin state change to separate AP-1's role in establishing, maintaining, and reading out memory, and identify any dose threshold.

title: Lineage-tracked inheritance test through division and passaging
description: Shard mechanism (sourdough starter keeps a community alive through periodic discarding): persistence through repeated partial removal indicates a self-propagating state. Prime cells with an AP-1 stimulus, then serially passage them with strong dilution, using barcoded lineages and single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) with live AP-1 reporters. Test whether the primed state persists, is heritable by clone, and re-establishes after dilution without the stimulus, and whether it needs continued AP-1 binding (acute degron versus none) to be passed on.

title: Stimulus-history order permutation with chromatin readout
description: Expose cells to many different orderings of the same pulses (e.g., TNF, EGF, stress, or phorbol ester), with each ordering changing only one adjacent step, as in change ringing. Then measure ATAC-seq accessibility at AP-1 (FOS/JUN) motif sites and the transcriptional response to a common test challenge. If the response depends on order and not just total dose, AP-1 is acting as a history-dependent memory.

title: Pioneer-like AP-1 'scar' mapping and persistence assay
description: Use CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for FOS, JUN, and H3K27ac, plus ATAC-seq, at several times after a transient stimulus, to find enhancers that stay open after AP-1 has left. Treat these residual 'repaired' sites as the signal, and test whether their persistence predicts a stronger secondary response. Acute degron removal of AP-1 (dTAG or AID) after priming then tests whether maintenance needs continued AP-1 binding or only the initial engagement.

title: Live single-cell reporter of AP-1 dynamics with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter, across cell divisions and re-stimulations. Treat cell-to-cell variability as the signal, and ask whether sister cells share activation states more than random pairs, and for how many generations. Use mutual information between past and future responses to quantify memory, and compare it with a control in which AP-1 dynamics are optogenetically clamped.

title: Optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 imprinting with sufficiency tests
description: Drive JUN/FOS with a light- or drug-inducible system using pulse patterns that differ in duration, frequency, and dimer composition. Then remove the input and track target gene expression, chromatin state, and responsiveness to later challenges. Sufficiency of a defined pulse pattern to create a lasting, heritable state, along with dependence on dimer identity, would test AP-1 as a causal memory writer rather than a correlate.

title: Perturbing the observer: feedback and cofactor dissection of memory maintenance
description: Test whether memory lives in AP-1 itself or in the system around it by combining CRISPRi/dominant-negative (A-FOS) of AP-1 with perturbation of cofactors and the chromatin machinery (SWI/SNF, p300, histone methyltransferases) and of the FOS/JUN positive-autoregulatory loop. Measure memory half-life after each perturbation, and use mathematical modelling to separate bistable feedback from epigenetic-mark inheritance. Finally, graft AP-1 sites into a synthetic locus to test whether the motif alone can store state.

title: Transient stimulus with chromatin accessibility memory readout (ATAC/CUT&Tag)
description: Give cells a brief inflammatory or injury stimulus (e.g., TNF or wounding), wash it out, and profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility by CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq at days 0, 1, 7 and 28. Like the 'fallway' (a path worn by prior use) in the material, persistently opened AP-1 motif sites in primed cells would show a trace of past stimulation. Compare these sites with sites in naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during and after priming
description: Use a degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN or FOS, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, to deplete AP-1 either only during priming or only after the stimulus has been removed. If AP-1 is needed to establish memory but not to maintain it, the primed state should persist after depletion in the later window. If it is needed for maintenance, the state should decay. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Re-stimulation response test with single-cell multiome
description: Prime cells, rest them, then re-challenge. Measure faster or stronger induction of target genes with scRNA-seq plus scATAC, and link it to the AP-1 motif accessibility of individual cells. Naive cells are the control, and a non-AP-1 priming stimulus is a second control. A memory mechanism predicts a heterogeneous but heritable primed subpopulation whose response scales with its retained AP-1 sites.

title: Lineage-tracing of memory through cell division
description: Track daughter cells with live reporters (a fluorescent AP-1 activity reporter, or endogenous FOS/JUN knock-in tags) and barcoded lineages after a pulse stimulus. Test whether sister cells share the primed state for several divisions, and whether mitotic bookmarking by AP-1 on chromatin (imaged or by mitotic ChIP) explains it. Such inheritance would separate true memory from a lingering signal.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and mathematical modeling of bistability
description: Use dCas9 to open or close one AP-1-bound enhancer, and fit an ODE model of AP-1 feed-forward and positive-feedback loops with chromatin states. The model predicts hysteresis, with different response thresholds on the way up and the way down. Test it by dose-response titration of the stimulus, and check whether editing a single site shifts or abolishes the memory.

title: Transient stimulus, delayed re-challenge ('hornbook' priming test)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury signal), remove it, then re-stimulate after days to weeks and compare transcriptional responses to naive cells. Measure ATAC-seq, RNA-seq and FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN) to see whether AP-1-dependent primed or enhanced responses persist after the AP-1 protein levels return to baseline.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either only during priming or only after priming, before re-challenge. If memory persists after AP-1 removal, AP-1 is only the initiator. If it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory. Readouts are chromatin accessibility and the secondary response.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of chromatin and expression states
description: Run paired scATAC/scRNA-seq at multiple times after stimulation and after resting. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility, AP-1 target expression and enhancer states are inherited by daughter cells, using lineage barcodes or sister-cell pairs to separate heritable memory from persistent signaling.

title: Enhancer-level epigenetic readout and engineered AP-1 sites
description: Map H3K27ac, H3K4me1, DNA methylation and nucleosome remodeling (BAF) at AP-1 bound enhancers before, after and long after stimulation. Then use dCas9 or motif mutation to delete or insert AP-1 sites at selected enhancers, to test whether binding is sufficient and necessary to leave a persistent open, primed state.

title: Live-cell reporters and mathematical modeling of feedback
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a downstream reporter in single cells during pulses of different duration and frequency.
