Fit bistable or positive-feedback models and test predictions, such as hysteresis and a threshold dose, by perturbing feedback loops (e.g., JUN autoregulation) to see if AP-1 dynamics alone can store state.

title: Haploid degron-based memory erasure (haploid undolorous / terminator)
description: Use haploid cells with an auto-inducible degron on FOS/JUN family members (a 'terminator' of AP-1), and deplete AP-1 at defined times after a transient stimulus. Then measure whether the stimulus-induced chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and the faster transcriptional re-response persist without AP-1 (memory is AP-1-independent) or decay (AP-1 maintains it).

title: Stimulus–rest–restimulus time course with dose and interval series (testing/gamely re-challenge)
description: Give a priming stimulus, wash it out, and re-challenge after varied intervals, measuring nascent RNA (PRO-seq) and target gene induction kinetics. A memory mechanism predicts primed cells respond faster or stronger, with a decay half-life that can be compared between wild-type and AP-1 perturbed cells.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporters (instructor-style lineage tracking)
description: Track AP-1 activity with live reporters or a FOS-GFP knock-in across cell divisions and lineages. Test whether the active or primed state is inherited by daughter cells more than expected by chance, and whether it correlates with later responsiveness.

title: Pioneer-like binding and chromatin state profiling (hiveward: following sites over time)
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP for JUN/FOS and for H3K27ac and H3K4me1, together with ATAC-seq, before, during and after stimulation. Identify enhancers that stay AP-1 bound or open after the signal is gone, and test whether those sites are the ones that drive faster re-induction.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-associated sites (CRISPR dissection)
description: Use dCas9 inhibition or activation, or motif mutagenesis, at persistently accessible AP-1 sites. Test necessity and sufficiency by asking whether editing the AP-1 motif abolishes the primed response at that locus, and whether forcing AP-1 binding in naive cells induces a primed state without a stimulus.

title: Transient stimulus then recall: AP-1 chromatin accessibility memory
description: Give cells a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA or a wound-like signal), wait until AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for H3K27ac, and transcription between naive and primed cells. Like 'patination' (a surface that records past exposure), persistent accessible sites that remain after the trigger is gone, and faster or stronger re-induction there, would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times (necessity for maintenance vs. establishment)
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative A-FOS, removed either during priming, during the rest period, or at re-stimulation. If memory needs AP-1 only during priming but not for later maintenance, it is an initiator. If memory is lost when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, AP-1 is a maintainer.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking with lineage barcodes
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq with live reporters of AP-1 activity and heritable barcodes across divisions after a transient stimulus. Test whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells and whether it correlates with the AP-1 motif accessibility of a clone, separating a stable epigenetic state from ongoing signaling noise.

title: Pioneer-like binding and nucleosome remodeling kinetics (footprinting, BRG1/BAF dependence)
description: Measure AP-1 occupancy by CUT&RUN or footprinting, together with BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment and histone marks, at primed loci over a time course after the stimulus is withdrawn. Test whether AP-1 sites stay open after AP-1 departs (hysteresis) by inhibiting BAF, and whether a mutated motif at an endogenous enhancer (CRISPR base editing) abolishes the memory.

title: Synthetic sufficiency and dose-history test with optogenetic AP-1 and a mathematical model
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic pulses of defined amplitude, duration and spacing, and read out reporter or endogenous gene responses over the following days. Fit bistability and hysteresis models, and test whether activation of AP-1 alone is sufficient to create a persistent state at naive loci that depends on pulse history and not just on current AP-1 levels.

title: Pulse-chase ATAC/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells briefly (e.g., TPA or serum), remove the stimulus, and profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility at defined time points over days. Sites that stay open after AP-1 binding has left (like the 'unpilfered' traces the word list hints at: structure remaining after the actor is gone) indicate AP-1-dependent memory, and can be compared with unstimulated controls.

title: Re-stimulation response test with AP-1 degron
description: Give a priming stimulus, rest the cells, then re-stimulate and measure transcription (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) of primed versus naive cells. Use an acute degron (dTAG/auxin) on FOS/JUN either during priming only or during re-stimulation only, to separate AP-1 as the writer of memory from AP-1 as the reader.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracking of memory persistence
description: Run scRNA+scATAC with a barcoded lineage label to follow primed clones through several divisions. Test whether accessibility and gene-expression states at AP-1 motifs are inherited by daughter cells more than expected from shared environment, using sister-cell concordance and decay rates.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and target gene state
description: Image a FOS/JUN fluorescent knock-in alongside MS2/PP7 or destabilised-reporter readouts of target loci during repeated pulses. Fit a quantitative model to see whether prior pulses change the amplitude, kinetics or bistability of later responses (hysteresis), which would be the signature of memory.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory sites and AP-1 motifs
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based tools (KRAB or p300) at the sites that stay open after priming, then test whether the primed response is lost, and whether forcing the site open without AP-1 restores it. Pair this with ChIP or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac and with pioneer-factor cofactors (e.g., BAF/SWI-SNF) to find the mechanism of persistence.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal chromatin accessibility time course (ATAC-seq + CUT&Tag)
description: Stimulate cells transiently (e.g., TNF, wounding, or inflammatory signal), then remove the stimulus and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and ATAC accessibility at its target enhancers over days to weeks. Persistent accessibility or H3K27ac at AP-1 motifs after AP-1 binding itself has decayed ('trabea' like a lingering vesting, a residual mark) would indicate AP-1-established memory, as in the epigenetic 'scars' of inflamed epithelium.

title: Acute degron depletion at priming vs. recall stages
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on FOS/JUN family members (or dominant-negative A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the first stimulus, during the rest interval, or only at re-stimulation. If depleting AP-1 only during priming abolishes the faster or stronger secondary transcriptional response, whereas depletion during rest has no effect, AP-1 is needed to write memory but not to maintain it; the opposite pattern shows it carries memory actively.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/history barcoding
description: Perform paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on cells with and without prior stimulation, with a heritable barcode or fluorescent AP-1 reporter recording previous exposure. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) and memory-gene expression stay correlated across cell divisions in clonal lineages, separating heritable (mitotically stable) memory from transient signaling noise.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter and optogenetic pulse patterning
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter while delivering controlled optogenetic or ERK-pulse inputs of varying duration, frequency, and rest interval. Fit input-history-dependent response curves (hysteresis, paired-pulse enhancement) to determine whether the system integrates past dynamics and for how long, giving quantitative memory timescales.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-associated AP-1 sites
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 epigenome editing or motif mutation at selected AP-1-bound enhancers (identified by persistent accessibility) after priming, and combine with Hi-C/Micro-C to look for retained loops. Test whether disrupting the AP-1 site or its recruited BAF/SWI-SNF chromatin remodeling erases faster re-induction of linked genes, establishing sufficiency and necessity at specific loci rather than genome-wide correlation.

title: Chromatin accessibility memory after transient stimulus (ATAC-seq time course)
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TNF, wounding, or growth factor), then wash out and profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at days to weeks. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motif sites after AP-1 binding has decayed would show AP-1 'opens' chromatin that is remembered, as in the 'reedbird' wordlist-like persistent marks (e.g., 'crackled' enhancer scars). Like a 'printed' imprint that remains after the stamp is lifted.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin-inducible degradation of c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS at defined windows: during the stimulus only, or only after the memory is established. If depleting AP-1 during induction abolishes the later enhanced response but depleting it afterward does not, AP-1 is needed to write but not to maintain memory (and vice versa), testing whether AP-1 itself stores the state.

title: Secondary-challenge functional assay with single-cell readout
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate and measure transcription of AP-1 target genes by scRNA-seq or live reporters, comparing to naive cells. Faster or stronger responses in primed cells, with and without AP-1 perturbation, quantify memory, and single-cell data reveal whether it is a graded or bistable, heritable state across cell divisions.

title: Pioneer-like binding and histone mark dynamics at AP-1 sites
description: Track H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and BAF/SWI-SNF (BRG1) occupancy with CUT&Tag over time at primed AP-1 sites, and test with AP-1 motif mutation via CRISPR base editing or dCas9 interference at selected enhancers. Mark persistence that requires the motif and recruited remodelers would show a mechanistic route from transient AP-1 binding to a lasting epigenetic state.

title: Mathematical modeling and optogenetic perturbation of AP-1 dynamics
description: Control AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemically induced pulses of varied duration and frequency, measure the resulting target gene state at later times, and fit ODE models of positive feedback (FOS/JUN autoregulation) versus chromatin-based memory. Model comparison, such as hysteresis and dependence on pulse number, discriminates network-based memory from epigenetic memory.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus ("unmask" latent enhancers)
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts) with a transient signal, then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints through weeks after washout. Memory is supported if AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and primed after stimulus clearance, analogous to 'unmasking' hidden regions, and give faster, stronger transcription upon restimulation.

title: Acute degron depletion of AP-1 during vs after priming
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS, depleting AP-1 either only during priming or only after priming (maintenance phase). If priming-phase loss abolishes the enhanced secondary response while maintenance-phase loss does not, AP-1 is needed for establishment but not for maintenance. The reverse pattern would show AP-1 itself maintains the memory.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/history tracing of AP-1 activity
description: Combine an AP-1 reporter or recorder (e.g., Cre-based or fluorescent timer under TRE elements) with scRNA/ATAC multiome to label cells that experienced AP-1 activity and follow them after rest. Test whether past AP-1 history predicts accessibility state and restimulation response in individual cells, separating cell-autonomous memory from population heterogeneity.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment sufficiency test
description: Use a dCas9-based or optogenetic system to transiently recruit AP-1 factors (or their pioneer-like partners) to a defined locus with a reporter. Then remove the trigger and measure whether accessibility, histone marks (H3K27ac/H3K4me1) and responsiveness persist across cell divisions. Persistence sufficient to alter later induction would show AP-1 can initiate memory by itself.

title: Live-cell imaging and kinetic modeling of AP-1 dynamics and division inheritance
description: Track endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with single-molecule or live imaging, and measure binding residence time, nuclear levels, and mitotic bookmarking across divisions in mother-daughter pairs. Fit mathematical models (bistable feedback vs. chromatin-based epigenetic memory) to see which explains retention and inheritance of responsiveness; AP-1 autoregulation (JUN induces JUN) is a natural positive-feedback candidate.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge (priming assay)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or PMA), let it wash out for hours to days, then re-stimulate and measure transcription of AP-1 target genes by RNA-seq and nascent RNA (PRO-seq). Like the 'compass that bends' and is echoed later, a faster or stronger second response, lost when AP-1 is inhibited, would show a memory that depends on AP-1. Compare naive, primed, and AP-1-depleted cells.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy tracking
description: Run ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac ChIP at time points before, during and long after the stimulus. Look for enhancers that stay open and AP-1-bound after the signal has gone, as if a 'mended atlas' retained a trace. Motif footprinting would show whether AP-1 binding persists or whether it only leaves behind an epigenetic mark.

title: Acute degron perturbation at defined memory phases
description: Fuse AP-1 subunits (c-JUN, FOSL1, or a dominant-negative like A-FOS) to a degron or place them under inducible control. Remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus (testing for establishment) or only after the stimulus ends (testing for maintenance), then re-challenge the cells. This separates AP-1 as a writer of memory from AP-1 as a maintainer, and it controls for the cells' general responsiveness.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporters with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or a fluorescent AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells across stimulation, rest, and re-stimulation, and follow daughter cells through divisions. Measure whether activity states persist, are heritable, and are bistable, using autocorrelation between mother and daughter cells. Fit the data to a mathematical model of positive feedback (JUN autoregulation) to test whether the memory is a cell-intrinsic state.

title: Targeted epigenome editing of AP-1 sites to test sufficiency and necessity
description: Use dCas9-based tools (KRAB or p300) or motif mutations through CRISPR base editing to alter specific AP-1-bound enhancers that stay accessible after the signal. Test whether closing them erases the primed response, and whether forced AP-1 binding or opening creates a memory without the stimulus. Readouts are the gene expression response to re-challenge and the persistence of chromatin marks, which would show causality at single loci.

title: Transient stimulus with long-delay re-challenge (primed response)
description: Expose cells to a brief AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or injury signal), let AP-1 activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate after days to weeks and measure transcriptional output by RNA-seq. Like the material's 'no chimney polishes the whistle twice', a memory would show as a changed second response compared with naive cells, and the change should depend on AP-1 (dominant-negative FOS/TAM67 or c-Jun degron).

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting
description: Run ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and H3K27ac before stimulation, after it, and after resolution. Test whether AP-1 motif-bearing enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 leaves, as the 'hinges remember' something. Persistence of accessibility at sites that were opened by AP-1 would be the key readout.

title: Acute degron depletion after the initial stimulus
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on JUN or FOS and remove the protein either during the priming stimulus or only during the maintenance period. If memory needs AP-1 only to establish it, removal during priming abolishes it and removal later does not. If AP-1 is also needed to maintain it, both abolish it. This separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Single-cell live reporters and lineage tracking
description: Image AP-1 activity reporters (e.g., a FOS-GFP knock-in or an AP-1 response-element reporter) and track cell lineages through divisions after a pulse. Test whether activity states are inherited by daughter cells more than expected from a random sibling pairing. Also use single-cell multiome data to link state heritability to chromatin.

title: Synthetic AP-1 pulse sufficiency test with locus-specific perturbation
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic JUN/FOS activation for defined pulse numbers, durations, and frequencies, and measure persistence of target gene expression and accessibility. Then use dCas9 to block AP-1 sites at one enhancer to test that site's necessity. Together these show whether AP-1 dynamics alone are sufficient to write a lasting state, and whether the memory is stored at specific loci.

title: Transient stimulus, delayed re-challenge (priming assay)
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), wait days to weeks after FOS/JUN levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq) against naive cells. Like the material's 'ledger' that remembers the marble, the readout is a stored record that changes later responses. Include AP-1 inhibitors (e.g., T-5224) or dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS) present only during the first stimulus to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish the memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting
description: Run ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors and H3K27ac at time points before, during and long after the stimulus. Check whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open after the AP-1 proteins have left, and whether they are the same loci that show the primed response. The 'braided ribbon' pattern is an interleaving of AP-1 binding with other pioneer or chromatin factors that keep sites open.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics with history
description: Use endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or AP-1 reporters in single cells, delivering pulses of different number and spacing. Test whether past pulses change later response amplitude (hysteresis) and whether the response is cell-autonomous and inherited by daughter cells after division. The 'rehearsing kite' idea: repeated practice changes later performance, which can be measured as a function of history.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-specific enhancers
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif mutation at candidate AP-1-dependent enhancers only after the initial stimulus, and optionally use acute degron tags (dTAG) to remove AP-1 at defined times. If memory is maintained by AP-1 continuously, late depletion should erase it. If AP-1 only writes memory, late depletion should not. This separates initiation from maintenance, like the 'hinge' that must be present to set a position but not to hold it.

title: Mathematical modeling and bistability tests
description: Build a model of AP-1 feedback (e.g., JUN autoregulation, with chromatin states) and fit it to dose-response and washout data. Test its predictions: bistability, a threshold dose for memory, and a hysteresis loop, with experiments such as dose titration and cell-sorting by AP-1 level. A 'lattice weighing its feather' suggests looking for a small stimulus change that tips a network between stable states.

title: Chromatin accessibility persistence after transient stimulus (ATAC-seq time course)
description: Stimulate cells briefly (e.g., TPA, TNF, or wounding), then profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at days to weeks after withdrawal. Like the 'tide forgets a salted garden' – a residue left after the tide recedes – persistent AP-1-motif-enriched open sites that outlast AP-1 occupancy would indicate a memory imprint.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 during priming vs. recall phases
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation of c-JUN/FOS (or dominant-negative A-FOS) only during the priming stimulus, only during the maintenance interval, or only during restimulation. Comparing secondary transcriptional responses separates AP-1 as the writer of memory (needed at priming) from the reader or maintainer (needed later), echoing the 'furnace swallows, thread weighs the vault' idea of an input that is stored and later weighed.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 activity and memory-gene response
description: Pair live-cell AP-1 reporters or single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with repeated stimulation to correlate each cell's first-pulse AP-1 dynamics with its second-pulse response. Each cell's history is a braided 'thread' of pulses, so the analysis tests whether AP-1 dose and duration predict a heritable, cell-autonomous response bias, including through cell division by lineage tracing.

title: Motif-mutation and dCas9 perturbation of AP-1 sites at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base-editing to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-KRAB/p300 to silence or activate specific enhancers, at candidate memory enhancers. Then test whether the primed chromatin state (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, accessibility) and faster re-induction are lost. Sufficiency can be tested by forcing AP-1 binding there with a synthetic recruiter and asking whether memory is created without the stimulus.

title: Cooperation with pioneer and chromatin remodelers: BAF dependence and histone mark kinetics
description: Perform time-resolved ChIP/CUT&Tag for SWI/SNF (BRG1/ARID1A), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 after AP-1 pulse and inhibit or degrade BAF during the memory interval. If AP-1 only initiates but remodelers keep sites open, accessibility will collapse upon their removal. This dissects whether memory resides in AP-1 itself or in the chromatin states it seeds, like a 'loom' retaining the pattern after the weaver leaves.

title: Prior-stimulus 'no ledger swallows twice' re-challenge assay
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or stress), rest them for days, then re-stimulate and measure transcription kinetics (nascent RNA-seq/PRO-seq) of AP-1 targets versus naive cells. Faster or stronger induction that depends on the first exposure, and that disappears when AP-1 (e.g., c-Fos/c-Jun) is acutely degraded during the rest period, would indicate AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy tracking (the 'engine borrows its spindle' test)
description: Run ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun family members, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) before stimulation, after it, and after a long washout. Check whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself is gone from them, which would show that AP-1 leaves a lasting chromatin imprint. Compare this with enhancers that revert.

title: Acute degron perturbation at defined time windows
description: Use dTAG/auxin degrons on JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-Fos, applied only during the initial stimulus, only during the maintenance period, or only at recall. This separates AP-1's role in writing memory from its role in maintaining it or reading it out. Readouts are persistence of accessibility and recall transcription.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and heritability
description: Track endogenously tagged Fos/Jun and an AP-1 reporter in single cells through stimulation, washout, and cell divisions. Test whether past activity predicts later responsiveness, and whether sister cells inherit similar states. Fit bistability or hysteresis models, such as feed-forward Jun autoregulation, to see if sustained states persist without the stimulus.

title: Enhancer-specific causal editing and sufficiency tests
description: Mutate or CRISPR-dCas9-block AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely tether AP-1 or chromatin-remodeler recruiters (e.g., BAF) to them by CRISPR. Then measure whether recall expression and the epigenetic state are lost or gained. Sufficiency of tethering without stimulus, and necessity of the motif, would be the strongest causal evidence.

title: Pulse-chase of AP-1 accessibility after transient stimulus
description: Give a brief stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding cytokine, or PMA) and map chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) ChIP/CUT&RUN at days 0, 1, 7, 21 after withdrawal. Like a pendulum whose lattice keeps a trace of the swing, persistent AP-1-bound open sites after signal loss would show an epigenetic trace; a faster secondary response at those loci would show it is functional.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the 'memory' phase
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS induced only after the priming stimulus is gone, then re-stimulate. If the enhanced transcriptional response disappears, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory and not only to establish it. Compare with degradation only during priming to separate writing from maintenance.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 reporter history
description: Image AP-1 activity reporters or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN in single cells through repeated stimulus pulses, and track lineages. Quantify whether the prior response predicts later amplitude or kinetics and whether the state is inherited by daughter cells, which separates cell-autonomous memory from population heterogeneity.

title: Chromatin-context and cooperation analysis at memory loci
description: Profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and DNA methylation, together with pioneer factors and SWI/SNF (BAF) occupancy, at AP-1 sites that stay open. Perturb the cofactors or the AP-1 motif by CRISPR, and test whether the site is a self-sustaining lattice (AP-1 recruits remodelers that keep the site accessible) or a passive mark.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 pulse and motif editing
description: Drive AP-1 optogenetically or chemogenetically with defined durations and doses in naive cells, and measure whether transient AP-1 alone leaves lasting accessibility and enhanced re-induction. Pair this with CRISPR deletion or mutation of individual AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers to test necessity at the locus level.

title: Transient stimulus then washout: persistence of AP-1 chromatin accessibility
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or keratinocytes) to a defined pulse of TPA, TNF or wounding signal, remove it, and track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN, and H3K27ac at AP-1 motif sites over days to weeks. Memory is supported if accessibility and a faster, stronger transcriptional response to restimulation persist after signaling and AP-1 levels return to baseline. This echoes the idea that 'no kettle echoes the tide twice': a second exposure should differ from the first.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate maintenance from initiation
description: Use dTAG or auxin-degron alleles of FOS, JUNB or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) at different times: before priming, during the memory phase, and just before restimulation. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, then removing it later spares the primed response. If it is needed throughout, then removing it later erases the primed response, which indicates a maintenance role.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage barcoding across divisions
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC on barcoded clonal lineages after priming and after several cell divisions. Test whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR deviation scores) and restimulation responses more than unrelated cells do. This shows whether the state is heritable rather than just long-lived protein or signaling.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporter memory
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN, and use an AP-1 target-locus reporter, in live single cells during repeated stimulation pulses. Quantify how the history of AP-1 dynamics (pulse number, interval) predicts later reporter output and the speed of reactivation. Compare to mathematical models of bistability or hysteresis, and check for a lingering, self-reinforcing loop.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and sufficiency tests at AP-1 sites
description: Use dCas9 to recruit or block AP-1 at specific primed enhancers, or mutate the motifs, with CRISPRi/a and base editing. Then test whether deposited marks and the primed response last without the original stimulus. Pair this with Hi-C or Micro-C to see whether AP-1-dependent enhancer–promoter contacts carry the memory. This tests whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient, and not merely correlated.

title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge ("no engine whispers twice")
description: Give cells a defined first pulse of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or injury cue), rest them for varying intervals, then re-stimulate. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent RNA) with naive cells to test whether AP-1 history changes the second response, and how long the change lasts. Include AP-1 loss (dominant-negative FOS/A-Fos, or degron) during the first pulse only, to show AP-1 is needed to set the memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 occupancy mapping
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for JUN/FOS, and H3K27ac at time points before, during and after the stimulus, through to weeks after it is withdrawn. Look for AP-1 motif sites that stay open or primed after AP-1 itself has left, as a "mended parchment" scar. Then test whether those sites predict the stronger or faster second response.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and persistence
description: Track endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or an AP-1 reporter, in single cells over repeated stimulations, using lineage tracing across divisions. Measure whether past AP-1 activity level, duration, or pulse pattern in a cell or its ancestors predicts the later response. This separates memory carried by cell state from population-level noise.

title: Targeted perturbation of memory-site enhancers
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif deletion at specific AP-1-dependent memory enhancers, either before the first stimulus or only between stimuli. If memory needs the site to be primed, silencing it before the first pulse should block the memory, whereas silencing it after should reveal whether it must be actively maintained. Add a gain-of-function arm, with synthetic AP-1 recruitment (dCas9-FOS) to a naive locus to see whether it can install memory.

title: Testing the maintenance mechanism: epigenetic and feedback contributions
description: Probe whether memory persists through chromatin remodelers (BAF/SWI-SNF), histone marks, or a positive feedback loop of AP-1 on its own expression. Inhibit these during the rest period and measure whether the primed state is lost, and use mathematical modelling of bistable or hysteretic AP-1 circuits to distinguish them. In vivo, test this in a tissue like regenerating or injured skin by comparing AP-1 conditional knockouts with controls on repeat injury.

title: Hysteresis curves from magnetic materials
description: Borrowing from ferromagnet physics, titrate a transient AP-1 stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ligand-induced c-Fos/c-Jun) up and then down, and measure target gene expression and AP-1 occupancy at each dose. A loop where the down-sweep differs from the up-sweep at identical input (path dependence) would show bistability and memory; compare to AP-1 dominant-negative (A-Fos) cells that should lose the loop.

title: Engram tagging from neuroscience
description: Use a Fos-driven Cre-ER/TRAP-style reporter to permanently label cells that experienced a prior AP-1 activation event, then re-stimulate days to weeks later and compare transcriptional response and chromatin accessibility between labeled and unlabeled cells by single-cell multiome. Faster, stronger, or qualitatively different responses in tagged cells would indicate AP-1-dependent priming memory.

title: Epidemic-style cell-lineage tracking (pedigree analysis from population genetics)
description: Time-lapse imaging of live AP-1 reporters in single cells with lineage tracing across divisions, then compute the autocorrelation of AP-1 activity between mothers, daughters and cousins, as in heritability estimates. Inheritance of activity state beyond what shared environment explains, after a transient pulse, would quantify mitotic memory and its decay half-life.

title: Molecular 'bookmarking' as in library cataloguing: mitotic chromatin profiling
description: Perform CUT&Tag/ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and enhancer marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) in mitotically arrested versus interphase cells after a prior stimulation, to test whether AP-1 stays bound to or leaves persistent accessible sites at specific loci. Pair with acute degron (dTAG) depletion of AP-1 after the stimulus to test whether maintenance of the accessibility state requires continued AP-1 presence versus only its initial pioneering.

title: Fault-tolerance testing from engineering: perturbation and rescue of the feedback circuit
description: Treat the AP-1 autoregulatory loop (FOS/JUN promoters containing TRE sites) like a flip-flop circuit: build a mathematical model, then experimentally test its predictions by breaking the loop (mutating TREs by CRISPR, using inducible degrons at varied timing) and measuring whether the active state persists, collapses, or can be reset. Model-guided discrimination between feedback-based memory and chromatin-based memory would be done by comparing persistence after degron removal at early versus late times.

title: Magnetic hysteresis loop for AP-1 dose-response
description: Borrowing from ferromagnetic hysteresis, expose cells to a ramped-up then ramped-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemically controlled FOS/JUN input) and measure AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and target gene expression along both paths. A non-overlapping loop, with residual signal at zero stimulus, would indicate path-dependent memory attributable to AP-1.

title: Immunological recall-response analogy: prime-challenge-rechallenge with AP-1 degron
description: Like vaccine prime/boost designs, give cells a first stimulus, rest them for variable intervals, then re-stimulate, measuring faster or stronger transcription at primed loci by nascent RNA-seq (PRO-seq). Acutely degrading (dTAG) AP-1 factors only during priming versus only during recall separates AP-1's role in establishing versus retrieving memory.

title: Neuronal engram-style lineage tracing of AP-1 history
description: Inspired by activity-dependent engram labeling (e.g., FOS-driven TRAP), use an AP-1-driven Cre or recorder to permanently tag cells that experienced AP-1 activation, then compare tagged and untagged sibling cells for later chromatin accessibility (scATAC) and response to re-stimulation. This tests whether past AP-1 activity predicts durable, cell-autonomous state differences.

title: Kinetic proofreading / persistence-time modeling from single-cell live imaging
description: Borrowing the signal-processing concept of memory kernels from physics and control theory, image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a transcription reporter in single cells over days, then fit autocorrelation and mutual-information decay times. Compare decay times with AP-1 protein half-life and chromatin mark half-life to see if persistence exceeds what protein turnover alone explains.

title: Epigenetic 'pioneer footprint' test using ecological succession logic
description: As in ecological succession, where early colonizers modify the habitat for later species, test whether AP-1 opens enhancers that remain accessible after AP-1 is removed. Perform time-course ATAC-seq, H3K27ac ChIP and motif analysis after stimulus withdrawal, and use dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or motif mutation at selected enhancers to test if accessibility persistence is AP-1-dependent and sufficient to enhance later responses.

title: Hysteresis curves from magnetic materials
description: Borrowing the physics of ferromagnetic hysteresis, titrate a stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or stress) up and then down, measuring AP-1 (FOS/JUN) levels and chromatin accessibility at target enhancers by single-cell ATAC/CUT&Tag at matched doses on each branch. Path-dependent output at identical input, which persists after the stimulus is removed, would indicate memory rather than simple tracking of the input.

title: Immunological recall-response design
description: Following vaccine prime-boost logic, give cells a primary stimulus, rest them for days to weeks, then give a secondary challenge and compare transcription kinetics and magnitude with naive cells. Pair this with time-course ChIP/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy and H3K27ac at 'primed' enhancers, and test whether AP-1 loss (dominant-negative A-FOS, degron) during priming only, or only during recall, abolishes the faster or larger secondary response.

title: Bistable switch tests from synthetic circuit engineering
description: Treat AP-1 positive autoregulation (JUN/FOS promoters bound by AP-1) as a candidate toggle switch. Use live-cell reporters of endogenous FOS/JUN and optogenetic or chemically induced pulses of varied duration to look for threshold behavior, bimodal single-cell distributions, and persistence of the ON state. Then break the feedback by mutating the AP-1 sites in the promoter and ask whether the memory is lost.

title: Lineage tracing and bookmarking, borrowed from mitotic inheritance in genealogy/pedigree analysis
description: Pedigree-style analysis: use time-lapse imaging of AP-1 reporters in sister and cousin cells after a transient stimulus to measure how the state is inherited over divisions, with correlation decaying by generational distance. Complement with mitotic-chromosome CUT&Tag and live imaging to test whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through mitosis (bookmarking) and whether the memory persists across divisions.

title: Archaeological stratigraphy of chromatin: ordered-dating of enhancer history
description: Like dating layers in an excavation, apply sequential perturbations (stimulus A then B, or reversed order) and map the AP-1 motif-containing enhancers that become newly accessible. Use footprinting, motif-resolved ATAC and Hi-C/Micro-C to resolve which sites are 'laid down' by the first stimulus and persist after AP-1 is removed, and test sufficiency by reinstating AP-1 at the site (dCas9 recruitment) in naive cells to see whether it recreates the remembered state.

title: Hysteresis curves from magnetic physics
description: Borrowing the magnetic hysteresis loop, ramp a stimulus (e.g., serum, TNF, or Ras/ERK activity via optogenetics) up and then down, and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy, chromatin accessibility and target transcription at matched stimulus levels. A path-dependent loop, with different output on the way up than on the way down, would indicate memory, and the loop area quantifies its strength.

title: Immunological recall-style prime-challenge design
description: Borrowing from vaccine prime-boost and trained immunity experiments, prime cells with a transient stimulus, rest them for varying intervals, then re-challenge. Compare ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for AP-1 and H3K27ac, and the speed and amplitude of the transcriptional response to naive cells, with and without acute AP-1 degradation (dTAG/dominant-negative A-FOS) during priming versus during recall to separate establishment from maintenance.

title: Information-theory channel capacity of single cells
description: Borrowing from communication engineering, use live-cell reporters of FOS/JUN dynamics and target genes in single cells, then compute mutual information between past stimulus history and current state after the stimulus ends. Memory is shown if state retains information about past input beyond a decay time, and the analysis can be compared with perturbations of AP-1 dimer composition.

title: Epigenetic bistability modeled like ferromagnetic domain switching
description: Borrowing from Ising or bistable-switch models in statistical physics, fit a mathematical model of AP-1 binding, pioneer-like nucleosome opening and positive feedback (e.g., FOSL1/JUN autoregulation) to time-resolved data. Test the model's predictions of bistability and critical stimulus thresholds by single-cell sorting of ON/OFF subpopulations and tracking their persistence through cell divisions.

title: Lineage barcoding like geological strata dating
description: Borrowing from stratigraphy, where layers record past events, combine lineage barcoding with a mark of AP-1 activation (e.g., a Cre- or recorder-based AP-1-responsive tag) to record which cells experienced past AP-1 activity. Then use single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) to test whether tagged cells and their descendants keep distinct accessible AP-1 motif landscapes and expression compared with untagged siblings, over many divisions.

title: Magnetic hysteresis loop for AP-1 chromatin state
description: Borrowing from ferromagnetic hysteresis, titrate a stimulus (e.g., FOS/JUN induction via optogenetic or dox-controlled dosing) up and then back down, measuring AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) at target enhancers. A path-dependent, non-retracing response at matched input levels would show AP-1-dependent memory, and acute degron removal of AP-1 would test whether the retained state requires it.

title: Immunological recall-style prime/rest/rechallenge with kinetic fitting
description: Borrowing from vaccine prime-boost design, expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA or a mechanical/inflammatory cue), rest them for variable intervals, then re-stimulate. Measure faster or stronger transcription of AP-1 target genes (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) and fit decay curves to estimate memory half-life, with and without dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) during priming only.

title: Epidemiological lineage tracing via barcoded clonal inheritance
description: Borrowing from cohort studies that follow families across generations, use lineage barcoding with live AP-1 reporters to follow sister cells after a transient stimulus. Compute intra-clonal versus inter-clonal correlation of AP-1 activity and target-gene expression across divisions, with the heritability of state quantifying mitotic memory.

title: Electronic flip-flop (bistable circuit) analysis through single-cell dynamics
description: Borrowing from digital memory circuits, test whether AP-1 with its positive feedback (FOS/JUN promoter autoregulation) forms a latch. Use live single-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters and a pulse-width/amplitude scan to look for bimodality, a switching threshold, and persistence after input withdrawal. Then perturb the feedback loop (e.g., mutate AP-1 sites in the JUN promoter) to see whether bistability collapses.

title: Archaeological stratigraphy of enhancer layers using time-resolved multi-omics
description: Borrowing from dating of layered deposits, perform time-course ATAC-seq, histone mark ChIP (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), and AP-1 motif-footprint analysis after a stimulus is removed, to define which enhancers stay in 'residual' accessible states. Then use CRISPRi/dCas9 editing of AP-1 motifs at these sites and ask causally whether the retained accessibility and the primed response of linked genes depend on the AP-1 sites.

title: Magnetic hysteresis loop for AP-1 chromatin state
description: Borrowing from ferromagnet hysteresis, expose cells to a rising then falling dose of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun activation) and measure ATAC-seq accessibility and target gene expression at matched doses on both the up and down ramps. Non-overlapping loops at AP-1 motif-containing enhancers, persisting after AP-1 levels return to baseline, would indicate memory rather than simple tracking of the input.

title: Neuronal long-term potentiation-style spaced-pulse training
description: Borrowing from the spaced-versus-massed learning paradigm, deliver optogenetic AP-1 pulses with the same total dose either massed or spaced, then challenge cells days later with a weak stimulus. Compare the secondary response (transcription, accessibility) between the two regimes to test whether AP-1 encodes stimulus history and shows learning-like kinetics.

title: Epidemiological case-control design via lineage barcoding
description: Borrowing from cohort studies, tag individual cells with heritable barcodes, expose the population to a transient stimulus, and track clonal lineages with single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) plus AP-1 footprinting. Test whether sister cells share AP-1-linked accessibility and expression states for multiple divisions, and whether the shared state predicts later responsiveness, which separates heritable memory from stochastic noise.

title: Molecular "knockout of the keystone" analysis from ecology: acute degradation after priming
description: Following ecological keystone-removal experiments, prime cells and then acutely degrade AP-1 (dTAG/auxin degron on c-Jun or FOSL) at different times after priming. If the primed accessibility and enhanced re-induction persist without AP-1, the memory is stored elsewhere (e.g., histone marks). If the memory decays, AP-1 is required for maintenance, not just initiation. CUT&RUN for H3K27ac/H3K4me1 and AP-1 binding maps what remains.

title: Bistable switch modeling from systems engineering with single-cell time-lapse
description: Borrowing control-theory concepts of positive feedback and bistability, use live reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., a Fos-GFP knock-in or AP-1 synthetic reporter) in single cells. Fit ODE or Bayesian models to the dynamics after transient stimulation, to test for bimodal, self-sustaining states. Perturb feedback nodes (e.g., FOS/JUN autoregulation, MAPK inhibition) to confirm that memory arises from circuit architecture, and compare model predictions with held-out perturbations.

title: Magnetic hysteresis loop for AP-1 dose-response
description: Borrowing from ferromagnetic hysteresis, expose cells to ramping-up then ramping-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or ERK/JNK activation driving FOS/JUN) and measure single-cell AP-1 target expression and chromatin accessibility on both paths. A non-overlapping loop, with residual 'remanence' after the stimulus returns to zero, would show state-dependent memory rather than simple input tracking.

title: Ecological resilience: perturbation-recovery and tipping-point analysis
description: Using the concept of alternative stable states and critical slowing down from ecology, apply pulses of varying strength and duration to cells and track recovery time and variance of AP-1 activity (live FOS/JUN reporters). Rising recovery time near a threshold and bimodal persistence of the primed state would indicate bistability supporting memory.

title: Library-style 'bookmarking' ChIP/CUT&Tag and ATAC time series
description: Inspired by bookmarks that hold your place after a book is closed, map AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy and accessibility at enhancers days after stimulus withdrawal and through cell division (mitotic chromosomes vs. interphase). Sites that remain open and AP-1-bound, and that respond faster on restimulation, mark AP-1 dependent memory loci.

title: Immunological secondary-response challenge with AP-1 degron
description: Like vaccine prime-boost designs, prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second challenge and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells. Use acute degradation (dTAG/auxin) of AP-1 factors or dominant-negative A-FOS only during priming versus only during rest versus only during boost to dissect whether AP-1 is needed to establish, maintain, or read out memory.

title: Computer-memory write/read test using synthetic AP-1 sites
description: Treating a genomic locus as a memory bit, insert a reporter flanked by wild-type versus mutated AP-1 motifs (or with dCas9 recruitment of FOS/JUN) and test whether a transient 'write' pulse yields stable ON state over many divisions, read out by flow cytometry and single-cell lineage tracking. Adding a pioneer-factor-free control and inhibitor of chromatin remodelers (BAF) tests whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to store the state.

title: Hysteresis curves borrowed from magnetic materials
description: Treat AP-1 chromatin state like a ferromagnet: ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or titrated FOS/JUN induction or MAPK activity) up and then down, and measure AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription at matched input levels. A non-overlapping up/down response loop that persists after the stimulus is removed would indicate history-dependent memory, and the loop width could be quantified per locus.

title: Immunological recall-style prime–rest–rechallenge design
description: Borrowing from vaccine prime/boost logic, expose cells to a transient stimulus (priming), allow a defined rest period, then rechallenge. Compare the kinetics and amplitude of target gene induction and AP-1 occupancy in primed vs naive cells. Include AP-1 dominant-negative (e.g., A-FOS) given only during priming vs only during rechallenge to separate the roles of AP-1 in establishing vs executing memory.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing as in clonal population genetics
description: Use barcoded lineages with split-clone designs (as in fate-mapping studies of heredity): stimulate one sister arm and not the other, then use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression are more similar among sisters and across divisions than among unrelated cells. Estimating heritability of the state across generations, analogous to the heritability estimates in quantitative genetics, would show whether it is mitotically stable.

title: Bistable switch modeling and live reporters from electrical circuit engineering
description: Build a dynamical-systems model of AP-1 with positive feedback (FOS/JUN autoregulation, with cooperating pioneer factors) and fit it to live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., a fluorescent AP-1 reporter and endogenous FOS-tagged knock-ins) measured across single-cell trajectories. Test the model's predictions of bistability (bimodal distributions, critical slowing down near thresholds, and flipping upon brief pulses). Then perturb feedback loops to see whether memory is lost.

title: Ecological succession-style locus-level perturbation and nucleation tests
description: Just as ecologists remove a keystone species to test whether a community can recover, use dCas9-based degradation or motif mutation at selected AP-1 sites after stimulation is removed, i.e., after the state has been set. Measure whether neighboring chromatin marks (H3K27ac, accessibility) and gene expression persist, collapse, or are rebuilt. Combine with AP-1 degron (dTAG) timing experiments to determine whether continuous AP-1 presence is required to maintain the state (a maintenance factor) or whether it only initiates a self-sustaining state (a trigger).

title: Gridiron-style compensation: paired AP-1 factor perturbation
description: Harrison's gridiron cancels opposing expansions, so a memory readout should be robust to nuisance drift. Acutely degrade or inhibit AP-1 (e.g., dTAG degron of FOS/JUN, dominant-negative A-FOS) at different times after a priming stimulus, then quantify chromatin accessibility and transcriptional response on restimulation. Compare this against a counter-perturbation that boosts the opposing factors, to show that AP-1 is needed specifically to maintain the primed state and not just to induce it.

title: Escapement-style pulse-train stimulation with live AP-1 reporters
description: A clock converts a steady force into discrete ticks, so test how AP-1 responds to pulsed versus sustained stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or growth factor pulses of varied frequency and spacing). Track FOS/JUN dynamics live with endogenous knock-in reporters, and ask whether the response to a second pulse depends on the interval since the first. A decay time constant that lasts days after the stimulus is gone would support memory.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 motif accessibility across a prime–rest–restimulate time course
description: Run scATAC and RNA-seq at baseline, after priming, after a long rest, and after restimulation. Use chromVAR and footprinting to ask whether AP-1 binding sites opened by priming stay open during rest and whether they predict faster or stronger gene induction. Link this to cell lineage barcodes, so that heritable memory across divisions can be separated from persistence in non-dividing cells.

title: Quartz-style halving test: memory persistence through cell division
description: Quartz divides a fixed frequency down to a countable beat. In the same way, follow primed cells through a defined number of divisions, using dye dilution or a division-tracking reporter. Measure AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and the primed response after 0, 1, 2 and more divisions. Check whether memory halves with each division, which would indicate dilution, or is stably re-established, which would indicate a self-propagating mechanism.

title: Sufficiency test with synthetic AP-1 site editing and transient pioneer-like recruitment
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or to recruit dCas9–FOS/JUN transiently, then remove the trigger. Measure whether enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac and enhanced gene induction persist after AP-1 is gone. Persistence would show AP-1 can write memory. Loss of memory when only the motifs are mutated would show the sites are necessary.

title: Flash-pattern decoding of AP-1 dynamics (live-cell reporters)
description: Like a lighthouse's identity is its on/off pattern, not its brightness, image live-cell AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS/JUN-tagged or AP-1 transcriptional reporters) after transient stimuli of different duration and frequency, then test whether pulse patterns (not just amplitude) are encoded and whether they predict later gene expression and cell fate. Compare with single-cell memory of the pattern after a washout period.

title: Priming-and-rechallenge assay with AP-1 degron
description: Give cells a first stimulus (e.g., growth factor, TPA, or inflammatory cue), rest them for days, then rechallenge and measure the enhanced or altered transcriptional response by RNA-seq. Use an acute degron (dTAG/auxin) on FOS/JUN family members during priming only versus rechallenge only, to separate AP-1 needed to write the memory from AP-1 needed to read it.

title: Chromatin accessibility 'ring' footprinting of AP-1 sites over time
description: Like Fresnel keeping only the active faces, focus on the minimal functional elements: run ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 motifs, H3K27ac, and BAF/pioneer markers before, after, and long after stimulus to find enhancers that stay open after AP-1 levels return to baseline. Test whether persistence depends on AP-1 motif integrity using CRISPR motif mutation or dCas9 interference at selected enhancers.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA plus ATAC with a lineage barcode in stimulated and unstimulated populations, and measure whether sister cells share AP-1 target accessibility and expression states after multiple divisions. Quantify heritability (sister-cell correlation versus random pairs) and whether it decays, which distinguishes epigenetic memory from persistent signaling.

title: Sufficiency test via transient AP-1 induction and positive-feedback mapping
description: Use optogenetic or inducible pulses of c-Jun/c-Fos in naive cells and check whether a self-sustaining state emerges, as with a lamp that needs no keeper to keep turning, by measuring endogenous JUN/FOS autoregulation, target gene persistence, and enhancer state weeks later. Perturb the loop (mutate AP-1 sites in the JUN promoter, block signaling kinases such as JNK) to determine if memory requires feedback versus continuing upstream input.

title: Flash-pattern decoding: AP-1 dynamics as a 'characteristic'
description: Like a lighthouse's identity encoded in its flash sequence, stimulate cells with pulsed vs sustained signals (optogenetic or ERK/JNK-activating pulses of defined count and interval) and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) live-reporter dynamics and downstream gene sets. Test whether distinct temporal patterns yield distinct, persistent chromatin and transcriptional states, indicating the pattern is stored and not just transiently read.

title: Fresnel-style minimal-footprint chromatin profiling
description: Fresnel kept only the functional surface of the lens; analogously, use CUT&Tag/ATAC-seq at single-cell resolution to find the minimal set of AP-1-bound enhancers that stay accessible after the stimulus ends. Compare accessibility, AP-1 motif occupancy and H3K27ac at these sites days after a transient stimulus versus naive cells, and ask whether this reduced set suffices to predict the primed response.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times after stimulus (keeper removal test)
description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation of FOS/JUN family members or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) at different times after the priming stimulus. If memory persists after AP-1 is removed, AP-1 only initiates it; if secondary responses and accessibility collapse, AP-1 actively maintains it, so compare these outcomes across timepoints.

title: Daymark/nightmark dual-readout of memory: re-stimulation response and sites
description: A lighthouse has two signaling systems for two conditions; likewise, compare the same cells by two readouts, namely the faster, stronger transcriptional response on re-stimulation (RNA-seq/nascent PRO-seq) and the persistent chromatin marks seen without stimulation. Correlate them per locus and per cell, and test causality by CRISPR-mutating AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers to see whether both readouts are lost together.

title: Lineage tracing of memory across divisions (mercury-bath inertia test)
description: Track primed cells through multiple cell cycles with live AP-1/target reporters and barcoded lineages or sister-cell comparisons, measuring how many divisions the primed state lasts and whether sisters inherit it equally. Combine this with mitotic-bookmarking assays (live imaging and mitotic ChIP) to check whether AP-1 stays bound to chromatin through mitosis, and add decay-rate modelling to separate heritable memory from slowly decaying signaling.

title: Fresnel-style minimal-essential chromatin footprinting
description: Like a Fresnel lens keeping only the light-bending surface, strip AP-1 sites down to what carries memory: use CUT&Tag/ATAC-seq plus motif-mutant and dCas9-based perturbations to find which AP-1-bound enhancer elements (c-Jun/Fos occupancy, H3K27ac, BAF-dependent accessibility) persist after stimulus removal. Then test whether this minimal set is necessary and sufficient for faster re-induction of target genes.

title: Prime–rest–restimulate with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TNF, EGF, or wounding signals), wait varying rest periods, and restimulate, measuring transcriptional response by nascent RNA-seq. Use dTAG/auxin degrons on FOS/JUN at defined windows (during priming vs. during rest vs. during restimulation) to determine whether AP-1 is needed to establish, maintain, or read out the memory.

title: Lighthouse 'characteristic' dynamics: live-cell AP-1 pulse decoding
description: Lighthouses are identified by flash patterns, so test whether AP-1 encodes history in its temporal pattern. Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and AP-1 reporters in single cells under optogenetic or microfluidic pulses of varied frequency and duration, then relate prior pulse patterns to later response amplitude and persistence, using information-theoretic measures.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Pair single-cell ATAC+RNA with lineage barcodes to follow sister cells after transient stimulation. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR) and target expression are shared among clonal relatives more than expected, and persist across divisions, which would indicate heritable memory, compared with transient states.

title: Bistability and hysteresis modeling with synthetic AP-1 circuit
description: Build a synthetic or engineered positive-feedback AP-1 locus, such as a JUN autoregulatory loop, and measure input–output curves in forward and reverse dose sweeps to detect hysteresis. Fit mathematical models and perturb feedback (mutate the JUN promoter TRE site, block pioneering cofactors) to show whether AP-1 feedback is required for self-sustaining states, like a weighted clock that keeps running after the push.

title: Rhythm-decoding: AP-1 dynamics as a temporal code
description: Like a lighthouse's long-short pattern identifying it, drive cells with optogenetic or chemically-gated ERK/JNK pulses of varied frequency and duration, and live-image FOS/JUN reporters. Then test whether pulse pattern (not just total dose) determines distinct downstream chromatin states and gene programs that persist after stimulation stops.

title: Chromatin-accessibility memory after transient stimulation
description: Stimulate cells once, wash out, and perform ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN, FOSL) and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at days 0, 1, 7, and 14 compared with naive cells. Persistent AP-1-bound, accessible 'primed' enhancers that give faster or stronger re-induction on second stimulation would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance (the 'bulk vs. surface' test)
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the first stimulus or only after the memory is established. If depleting during priming abolishes later re-response but depleting afterward doesn't, AP-1 is needed to write the memory; if later depletion also erases it, AP-1 maintains it.

title: Single-cell prime-and-rechallenge with lineage tracing
description: Prime cells, let them divide, and perform single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with barcoded lineage tracking to see whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility and response magnitude to a second challenge. Heritable clonal concordance of response, correlated with AP-1 occupancy, demonstrates mitotically stable memory rather than transient signaling.

title: Targeted enhancer perturbation and sufficiency test
description: Use CRISPRi/dCas9 or motif mutation to silence or edit AP-1 binding sites at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely tether AP-1 (dCas9-FOS/JUN) to naive loci. Measure whether the edits eliminate or create faster re-induction of the nearby gene, testing necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding for locus-specific memory.

title: Hysteresis loop test (catenary/expansion-joint analogy)
description: Stimulate cells with a graded dose series of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or growth factor), then withdraw it, and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression on the rising and falling arms. If AP-1 encodes memory, accessibility and expression should depend on stimulus history (hysteresis), as a bridge's length depends on the thermal cycle, and should not just follow the current input.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus (breaking step)
description: After a priming stimulus, use a degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 at different times, either during priming or after it has ended. Then re-stimulate and compare the secondary response. This separates AP-1 as the initiator of memory from AP-1 as the maintainer of it, and shows whether the memory state persists without continuous AP-1 occupancy.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of synchrony and heritability
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters or FOS/JUN imaging with lineage tracing across cell divisions, and with single-cell RNA plus ATAC. This tests whether primed cells pass on their state to daughter cells and whether neighboring cells synchronize through paracrine signals, as walkers on the Millennium Bridge did. It also shows whether memory is a bimodal cell-intrinsic state or a population average.

title: Pioneer-like footprinting and epigenetic coupling
description: Do time-course CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for AP-1 subunits, H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and BAF/SWI-SNF components, and measure nucleosome occupancy with ATAC footprinting at newly opened enhancers. Check whether the enhancers stay open and marked after AP-1 leaves, and whether motif mutation by CRISPR base editing removes the memory at that site only. This is like asking whether the structure keeps its new shape after the load has gone.

title: Feedback-loop modeling and perturbation (flutter-like self-feeding)
description: Build a dynamical model of AP-1 positive feedback, in which FOS/JUN transcription drives further AP-1 activity through autoregulation and signaling loops. Fit it to time-resolved data on protein levels and phosphorylation (JNK/ERK). Then test its predictions of bistability and of a critical stimulus threshold by perturbing feedback nodes optogenetically or with inhibitors, to see if memory persists as a self-sustaining state.

title: Fresnel-style minimal-core reduction: which AP-1 features carry the memory?
description: Like a Fresnel lens keeps only the surface curvature that bends light, strip AP-1 down to its minimal functional elements by using domain-specific mutants of FOS/JUN (DNA-binding, dimerization, and pioneer-like or chromatin-remodeler recruitment domains). Then test which element is required for a stimulus-induced chromatin accessibility state to persist after the stimulus is removed, measured by ATAC-seq and H3K27ac CUT&Tag over several cell divisions.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal persistence time course with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TPA, wounding signals, or inflammatory cues), then withdraw the stimulus. Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) to remove AP-1 factors at different times: during priming only, after washout only, or both. Track enhancer accessibility, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and target gene re-inducibility to separate AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a maintainer of the memory.

title: Lighthouse-signature dynamics: pulse-pattern encoding of memory
description: Lighthouses identify themselves by flash timing, so deliver identical total stimulus doses with different on/off patterns (e.g., 2 h on, 6 h off versus continuous). Do this using optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN, and read out with live-cell AP-1 reporters and single-cell RNA-seq or ATAC-seq. This tests whether AP-1 dynamics, not just level, determine whether a durable memory is written and how strongly secondary stimulation is primed.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory inheritance
description: Mark cells with a live AP-1 reporter or endogenous tagged FOS/JUN and a heritable barcode. After transient stimulation, follow sister cells through division and test whether the AP-1 state and accessible chromatin are shared more between sisters than between random cells. Then compare the response of memory-positive and memory-negative sister lineages to restimulation, and use the results to model mitotic bookmarking and inheritance.

title: Targeted write/erase of AP-1 sites at specific enhancers
description: Use dCas9-based recruitment, or deletion/mutation of AP-1 motifs, at candidate memory enhancers (for example, those near genes with faster second responses). Test whether adding AP-1 sites is sufficient to create a primed, faster-responding state, and whether removing them abolishes it, without altering the global stimulus. Measure local accessibility, histone marks, nascent transcription (PRO-seq), and kinetics of the secondary response to establish site-specific causality.

title: Fresnel-style minimal-sufficient chromatin footprint
description: Like a Fresnel lens keeping only the surfaces that bend light, identify which AP-1 binding sites and accessible enhancers are the minimal 'functional' elements retaining memory. Do ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN after a transient stimulus and after washout, then use CRISPR deletion or dCas9-KRAB on the persistently accessible sites to test which are necessary for a heightened secondary response.

title: Prime-rest-restimulate time course with AP-1 perturbation
description: Stimulate cells (e.g. macrophages or fibroblasts) once, rest them for days, then restimulate and measure transcriptional output by RNA-seq and nascent RNA. Compare primed with naive cells under dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) or degron-mediated acute JUN/FOS depletion applied only during priming versus only during restimulation, to separate AP-1 as the writer of memory from AP-1 as the reader.

title: Flash-signature dynamics: live single-cell AP-1 reporters
description: Lighthouse flash patterns encode identity through rhythm, so test whether AP-1 activity dynamics (pulse number, duration, frequency) encode and store history. Use live-cell FOS/JUN knock-in fluorescent reporters with optogenetic or pulsed stimulation of defined patterns, then relate pulse history to later response and to chromatin state in the same cells.

title: Bistability and hysteresis test of the AP-1 positive-feedback loop
description: A rotating lens on a mercury bath holds its state through low friction, so test whether AP-1 holds its state through self-reinforcement. Titrate stimulus up and then down and measure single-cell JUN/FOS levels by flow or imaging. A history-dependent, bimodal response (hysteresis) would show a self-sustaining state, and mathematical modeling plus feedback-loop disruption, such as mutating AP-1 sites in the JUN promoter, would test the mechanism.

title: Persistence and inheritance across cell division with epigenetic readouts
description: Test whether memory outlasts the signal and is passed through mitosis by tracking sorted primed cells and their daughters over several divisions. Measure AP-1 occupancy, H3K27ac, and BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment, and compare against the half-life of AP-1 proteins and mRNAs. Persistent accessibility without AP-1 would point to AP-1 as a trigger for chromatin-based memory, while loss of memory when AP-1 is removed would point to AP-1 itself as the carrier.

title: Acoustic-style single-event monitoring of AP-1 binding dynamics
description: Use live-cell single-molecule tracking or CUT&Tag time courses to detect individual FOS/JUN binding and dwell events at specific enhancers after a transient stimulus (like listening for single wire breaks). Test whether residence times and occupancy at 'memory' sites stay altered days after the stimulus ends, compared with naive cells.

title: Pluck-and-tension test: perturbation response probing of latent AP-1 state
description: Measure how cells respond to a small standardized re-stimulation (the 'pluck') at various times after a priming stimulus, reading out AP-1 target transcription, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and FOS/JUN levels. A faster or stronger response (frequency shifts indicating hidden load) in primed cells, which depends on AP-1 sites, would show a stored state not visible at baseline.

title: Pry-open the bundle: acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells, then use degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 at different times: during priming, during the memory interval, or only at re-challenge. Compare which windows abolish the enhanced secondary response and persistent accessibility, separating AP-1 as initiator versus maintainer of memory.

title: Strand-by-strand motif mutagenesis and single-cell heterogeneity
description: Use CRISPR editing or base editing of individual AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, plus single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) to resolve which 'strands' carry the memory. Test whether memory is lost per-site and whether cell-to-cell heterogeneity of retained accessibility predicts the strength of the later response and its inheritance through divisions.

title: Inspect the hidden crack: lineage tracing of memory through cell divisions
description: Track primed cells and their daughters by live imaging with AP-1 reporters or barcoded lineages, and check whether elevated accessibility and reporter state persist across several generations without ongoing stimulus. Pair this with measurements of histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and DNA methylation at AP-1 sites to find the mechanism that maintains the state, and compare with cells where division is blocked.

title: Tablebase-style exhaustive history mapping of AP-1 states
description: Like a tablebase that solves every position, systematically expose cells to a grid of stimulus histories (dose, duration, order of e.g. TNF, EGF, or TPA pulses). Measure the resulting AP-1 (FOS/JUN family) occupancy by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq, then test whether the final state depends on the path taken, which would indicate memory.

title: Zugzwang test: does AP-1 memory require active maintenance?
description: After a priming stimulus and a rest period, withdraw AP-1 acutely, using a degron on FOS/JUN or dominant-negative A-FOS, and see whether the primed enhancers lose accessibility and the faster secondary transcription. If memory is lost only when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, it is actively maintained. If it persists, the memory is passive and held by other factors.

title: Opposition-style paired-state live imaging
description: Build a live-cell reporter of AP-1 activity, for example an AP-1 response element driving a fluorescent protein together with a tagged JUN. Follow single cells through prime, rest and restimulation, and compare the response of primed and naive cells side by side. Measure how long the difference lasts and whether it is inherited by daughter cells, to separate true memory from a transient hold.

title: Pawn-promotion test: sufficiency by ectopic AP-1 priming
description: Use optogenetic or inducible AP-1 (e.g. dox-inducible c-Jun/FOS) to give a transient pulse in naive cells in place of the natural stimulus. Test whether the pulse alone converts enhancers to a persistent accessible state with H3K27ac and H3K4me1, and enhances later gene induction. Compare this with a mutant lacking its DNA-binding or transactivation domain.

title: Single-cell multiome with perturbation of AP-1 motifs
description: Perform paired scRNA and scATAC on primed and unprimed cells, using CRISPR deletion or mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers. Test whether motif accessibility and chromatin-state heterogeneity predict each cell's secondary response. Also test whether recruitment of SWI/SNF (BAF) or pioneer factors depends on those motifs, which would show a mechanism and not just a correlation.

title: Headway-style spacing of stimulus pulses
description: Deliver repeated stimuli (e.g., TNF, wounding cues, or optogenetic c-Jun/Fos) at varied intervals, like train headways, and measure whether chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene output at AP-1 sites on later pulses depend on interval. A memory-like mechanism predicts a minimum recovery interval and a persistence window, while a transient transcription factor does not.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 occupancy and accessibility after stimulus withdrawal
description: After a priming stimulus, track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding by CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at multiple time points over days to weeks, long after AP-1 activity returns to baseline. Persistent open enhancers at AP-1 motifs, without sustained AP-1 binding, would indicate AP-1 set a durable epigenetic state, like a standardized clock that outlasts the signal.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 during priming versus recall
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on c-Jun/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 only during the priming phase, only during the recall (second stimulus) phase, or both. If memory requires AP-1 only at priming but not at recall, it acts as a writer. If it is needed at recall too, it acts as a reader or maintainer.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory readout
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters or FOS/JUN imaging with barcoded lineage tracing and single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC). Test whether sister cells share primed accessibility and faster re-induction, which would show heritable memory through division, as opposed to a population-level transient response.

title: Motif perturbation and epigenome editing at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, and dCas9 tools to add or remove marks like H3K27ac or DNA demethylation, then measure the recall response. Loss of faster re-induction after motif mutation, with rescue by forced opening, would show causal sufficiency and necessity. Chromatin remodelers such as BAF could be tested as the maintenance link.

title: Bistable switch test via hysteresis (Kresling analogy)
description: Like a Kresling cylinder snapping between stable states, test whether AP-1 activity is bistable: expose cells to graded stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or inducible c-Fos/c-Jun) up and then down, and measure single-cell AP-1 reporter output and target genes. Hysteresis, bimodal distributions, and persistence of the high state after stimulus removal at identical doses would indicate a self-sustaining memory state; perturbing positive feedback (c-Jun autoregulation) should abolish it.

title: Chromatin accessibility memory of AP-1 sites (crease persistence)
description: A fold leaves a crease that persists after the force is gone; test whether transient AP-1 activation leaves lasting accessible chromatin. Do ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, H3K27ac and pioneer-like remodeler (BAF) occupancy at time points after stimulus washout across many cell divisions, and compare motif-defined AP-1 sites with other sites for retained accessibility and faster re-induction on restimulation.

title: Acute degron removal after priming (one-degree-of-freedom control)
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-degradable AP-1 subunit (c-Jun/FOS/FOSL) to deplete AP-1 at defined times: during priming, during the memory interval, or only at restimulation.
