If memory requires AP-1 presence in the interval, depletion then erases the faster secondary response. If only priming needs it, AP-1 acts as an initiator whose crease persists without it, separating initiation from maintenance by RNA-seq and nascent transcription (PRO-seq).

title: Dynamic encoding with optogenetic pulses and live reporters
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic or chemically timed pulses of varying duration, frequency, and number while imaging a live AP-1 reporter and a target gene (e.g., MS2 or fluorescent knock-in). Fit models comparing response to naive versus pre-pulsed cells, to quantify memory duration, dependence on pulse history, and whether cells integrate past inputs like a mechanical system with state.

title: Lineage-resolved single-cell multiome with memory-site mutagenesis
description: Combine single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) or barcoded lineage tracing on primed versus naive cells to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression are inherited by sister cells beyond cell division. Then use CRISPR to mutate or dCas9-block specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers (like altering a single hinge) and test whether that selectively removes the primed response while leaving other enhancers intact.

title: Fresnel-style decomposition of AP-1 occupancy into 'rings' by dimer composition
description: Like a Fresnel lens splitting one thick slab into concentric prisms that together do the same job, split AP-1 into its component Fos/Jun family dimers using CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for each member before, during and after a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA or injury). Test which dimers persist at enhancers after the stimulus is gone and whether persistence predicts faster or stronger re-induction of target genes.

title: Stimulus–washout–restimulation with chromatin accessibility readout
description: Give cells a defined pulse of signal, wash it out for varying intervals, then restimulate, and measure ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) at AP-1 motif sites. If AP-1 acts as memory, accessibility and the transcriptional response to the second pulse should depend on the first pulse and decay with a measurable half-life.

title: Acute degradation of AP-1 at different memory phases
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-Jun or Fos to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus only or during the memory (maintenance) interval only. If AP-1 is needed to establish but not to maintain the memory, enhancers should stay open after removal. If it is needed for both, accessibility and re-induction should be lost, which separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 activity with lineage tracking
description: Image an AP-1 reporter and endogenously tagged Fos/Jun in single cells and follow their progeny after a transient stimulus. Test whether reporter state is inherited across divisions, how long it persists, and whether sister cells stay correlated, as a heritable mechanism would predict and as noisy transient signaling would not.

title: Targeted perturbation of AP-1 motifs and chromatin state at individual enhancers
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs by CRISPR base editing, or recruit dCas9-based writers or erasers (p300, KRAB) to selected enhancers, then compare the primed-state response of edited and unedited alleles in the same cell. This shows whether the motif and the chromatin state it leaves behind are causal for memory, and whether the memory acts in cis on one allele.

title: Read-back test: AP-1 binding persistence after stimulus withdrawal
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts with TNF/TGF-β/LPS), withdraw the signal, and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq over days to weeks. Like pilots reading back a clearance to confirm it was received, this asks whether the AP-1 footprint is faithfully repeated at the same enhancers after the signal is gone and persists through cell divisions.

title: Odd/even lane test: acute AP-1 degradation at defined timepoints
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) c-JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the priming window or after the memory is established. If memory is stored by AP-1, removal during priming should block enhancer accessibility and faster secondary responses, while removal later should erase the memory. Measure the secondary transcriptional response by RNA-seq to separate AP-1's role in writing the memory from its role in maintaining it.

title: Handoff test: pioneer activity and chromatin-state succession
description: Profile H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and nucleosome remodeling (BAF/SWI-SNF, p300) at AP-1 sites over time to check whether AP-1 hands the site off to other factors or to epigenetic marks that then persist without AP-1. Combine with ChIP/CUT&RUN for co-factors and a time-resolved AP-1 depletion to see whether the mark outlasts AP-1 itself, which would indicate that AP-1 initiates memory but does not store it.

title: Single-cell and lineage-tracing of memory inheritance
description: Use single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with barcoded lineages or sister-cell pair live imaging with an AP-1 reporter (e.g., a FOS/JUN-driven reporter) to test whether the memory state and AP-1 activity are inherited across divisions, and whether they are correlated within clones. Compare the heritability of the response with the stability of the response in unrelated cells to separate true cellular memory from persistent signaling.

title: Sufficiency and site-specificity: motif editing and synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at a few memory-associated enhancers, and conversely use dCas9-based recruitment of JUN/FOS to a naive locus. Then ask whether a transient pulse at the locus alone creates durable accessibility and a stronger re-response. This tests the necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding for memory at specific loci, as opposed to global signaling effects.

title: Hysteresis test via transient stimulus and long washout
description: Expose cells to a brief, defined stimulus (e.g., TPA, serum, or a cytokine pulse) that induces FOS/JUN, then track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression for days to weeks after washout. Like a glacier that keeps flowing after the meltwater input changes, persistence of accessibility and transcription after AP-1 levels return to baseline would indicate memory, and a dose-response across pulse strengths would reveal hysteresis.

title: Time-gated AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative A-FOS, removing AP-1 at different times: before, during, or after the priming stimulus. If the primed state survives AP-1 removal after the establishment window, AP-1 is only an initiator; if it collapses, AP-1 is needed to maintain the state, as a continually running engine rather than a stored record. Readouts are ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and re-stimulation response.

title: Single-cell live reporter imaging with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenous AP-1 activity (knock-in FOS/JUN fluorescent tags plus an AP-1 transcriptional reporter) in single cells across stimulation, rest, and re-stimulation, tracking daughter cells through divisions. Quantifying whether past activity history predicts later response amplitude and whether the state is heritable through mitosis, with heterogeneity measured per cell and not averaged, would show memory as a cell-intrinsic, bistable property.

title: Motif-mutation and pioneer-like function at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base editing or enhancer deletion to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers that stay open after stimulation, then test if they still gain and retain accessibility, H3K4me1/H3K27ac, and faster re-induction. Pair with Micro-C or ChIP for BAF/chromatin remodelers to see whether AP-1 recruits remodelers that leave a lasting mark, like cryoconite pellets that melt their own hollows and leave them behind.

title: Memory-dependent response to second stimulus across contexts, with modeling
description: Compare primed and naive cells (e.g., in vitro and in vivo, such as inflamed vs. naive skin or epithelial stem cells) for the response to a second stimulus using RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and footprinting, then fit a mathematical model (positive feedback, chromatin-state variables) to the data. Perturbing predicted feedback components, such as AP-1 autoregulation or histone modifiers, tests if the model explains the persistence and distinguishes AP-1-driven memory from other mechanisms.

title: Two-bearing triangulation of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin state
description: Like two towers' bearings crossing at a fire, intersect two independent readouts at the same loci after a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury): AP-1 (FOS/JUN) ChIP/CUT&RUN occupancy and ATAC-seq accessibility or H3K27ac. Loci where both persist long after the stimulus ends, and AP-1 motif-containing sites are the only overlap, are candidate memory sites.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus has ended (necessity test for maintenance)
description: Prime cells, wash out the stimulus, and after a rest period add a dTAG/AID degron or dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 only during the memory phase. Compare accessibility and the faster secondary response on restimulation to controls; loss of memory when AP-1 is removed after induction shows AP-1 is required to maintain it, not only to establish it.

title: Sufficiency by optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 pulses
description: Drive FOS/JUN activity with a light- or drug-inducible system in naive cells using pulses of different duration and frequency, then measure persistent chromatin opening and altered transcriptional responses to a later unrelated stimulus. This tests whether AP-1 activity alone can write a lasting state and how its dynamics encode dose or history.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory persistence and heritability
description: Use live reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., FOS-GFP) with time-lapse imaging or barcoded lineages plus scRNA/scATAC to track whether primed state passes through cell divisions and how many generations it lasts. Like the lookout's logbook, this gives a time-stamped record per cell, showing whether the state is bistable or heritable versus a decaying signal.

title: Pioneer-like activity and cofactor dependence at primed enhancers
description: Mutate or CRISPR-delete AP-1 motifs at specific primed enhancers, and use CUT&Tag, BAF/SWI-SNF inhibition, and Micro-C to test whether AP-1 recruits remodelers and holds loops open. Reporter assays for memory (faster reinduction of the linked gene) will show whether site-specific AP-1 binding is causal, versus alternatives like other TFs or DNA methylation.

title: First-order reversal curves for AP-1 target loci
description: Drive cells with a ramp of AP-1 input (optogenetic or inducible c-Fos/c-Jun, or a defined stimulus dose), reverse at varied peak levels, then sweep back up. Measure single-cell reporter output (AP-1 activity, chromatin accessibility at target enhancers) to build a Preisach-like map of per-locus up and down thresholds, which tests whether hysteresis and bistable switching exist rather than simple graded responses.

title: Return-point and wiping memory test with nested stimulus histories
description: Apply stimulus sequences with nested maxima and minima, such as a small excursion inside a larger one, and then readout. Test whether the final chromatin or transcriptional state depends on the ordering of extreme amplitudes, not on timing, and whether larger excursions erase the imprint of smaller ones. Return-point memory would support a history-encoding mechanism rather than a transient signal.

title: Decay kinetics of the remembered state (viscosity analysis)
description: After a transient AP-1 pulse, measure accessibility, H3K27ac, and target expression over hours to weeks, with and without cell division. Fit log-time versus exponential decay, and use perturbations such as proliferation arrest, temperature, or BET/HDAC inhibitors to distinguish stable self-sustaining memory from slow forgetting (passive dilution or residual signalling).

title: Stepwise erasure and reprogramming by AP-1 dominant-negative and degron perturbations
description: At staged times after the priming stimulus, acutely remove AP-1 (A-Fos dominant negative, dTAG/auxin degron on c-Jun/FOSL) and track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN and RNA output. If the memory persists after AP-1 loss it is stored elsewhere; if it is lost it needs continuous AP-1. Like stepwise thermal demagnetization, this peels away layers by priming time and tests whether AP-1 is the carrier or only the writer.

title: Re-stimulation response test (Thellier-style comparison)
description: Prime cells in a known stimulus, rest, then re-challenge with a standard test dose and compare it with naive cells. Measure faster or larger induction, AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and accessibility at primed sites, and whether the effect scales with prior dose. Using matched naive controls and different priming doses allows the memory 'signal' to be calibrated and separated from later overprints, such as secondary signalling.

title: Hysteresis loop of AP-1 dose-response
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ERK input driving FOS/JUN) up and then down in single cells, and measure AP-1 activity and target-gene output (live reporters, chromatin accessibility) to see if the descending branch differs from the ascending one. A gap that persists after long waits, and decays logarithmically rather than exponentially, would indicate stable memory with many barriers rather than slow relaxation.

title: Remanence decay and erasure by decaying pulses
description: After a transient stimulus, track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target expression over days to weeks to get the decay kinetics. Then try to erase the memory with a shrinking-amplitude oscillating stimulus (analogous to AC demagnetization) or by acute degron removal of AP-1, to test whether AP-1 is needed for maintenance rather than only for initiation.

title: First-order reversal curve census of AP-1 sites
description: Apply stimulus histories with different peak and reversal levels, then read out accessibility or reporter activity at individual AP-1 enhancers. Fit a Preisach-style model with two thresholds per site to get the distribution of switching thresholds, and test return-point memory: cycle partway, return, and check whether the state is retraced exactly. This shows whether memory lives in independent enhancer switches or in their coupling.

title: Stepwise peeling of layered memory by order-of-exposure experiments
description: Expose cells to sequential stimuli (e.g., wounding, then inflammation, then a third signal) in different orders. Use time-resolved ATAC/CUT&Tag to see whether later AP-1 events overwrite or add to earlier accessible sites, and use stepwise degron depletion to peel back the layers. This tells you whether the memory is hierarchical and which earlier imprints a later stimulus can overwrite.

title: Switch versus coupling test via perturbation of cooperativity
description: Separate the contribution of individual AP-1 motifs from that of the surrounding network (positive feedback of FOS/JUN on its own promoters, pioneer cooperation with partner factors like ETS or the SWI/SNF complex). Mutate motifs at single enhancers by CRISPR, and block feedback loops or chromatin remodelers, then measure single-cell bistability and the persistence of the primed state. If memory is lost when coupling is cut but not when motifs are retained, it is a network property rather than a property of the individual sites.

title: Sweep-rate and relaxation controls for AP-1 hysteresis
description: Stimulate cells with graded, ramped doses of a signal (e.g., TPA, EGF, or anisomycin) up and down at several sweep rates, then read out AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN levels, a reporter, ATAC accessibility at AP-1 motifs). If loop width shrinks as the sweep slows, the apparent memory is just slow relaxation. If it persists at slow rates, it reflects a bistable or stored state. Add the same sweep to a JUN/FOS degradation-rate mutant to separate sluggish kinetics from true retention.

title: First-order reversal curve mapping of single-cell AP-1 thresholds
description: Drive cells partway up the dose axis, reverse, and repeat from many reversal points. Use live single-cell AP-1 reporters or multiplexed imaging to build a Preisach-like distribution of up- and down-switching thresholds across cells. A population of bistable cells with distinct thresholds would support a memory made of many two-state units, while a unimodal graded response would argue against it.

title: Return-point and erasure tests with decaying-oscillation stimulation
description: Give a pulse history with a defined peak, wiggle the stimulus inside that peak, and check whether AP-1 target gene output and chromatin state remember only the maximum, as in return-point memory. Test erasure by applying a slowly decaying oscillating stimulus or an inhibitor wash-out (e.g., a dominant-negative FOS such as A-FOS), and measure how much stimulus is needed to wipe the record. Compare the dose needed to erase with the dose needed to write.

title: Locating the pinning sites: AP-1 binding, chromatin, and mutation at the enhancer level
description: Map where memory is stored using CUT&RUN or ChIP for FOS/JUN, ATAC-seq, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at sites before, during, and after the stimulus. Then use CRISPR to mutate individual AP-1 motifs or degrade AP-1 with a degron after the stimulus, and ask whether enhancer accessibility and the response to a second stimulus persist without AP-1. This distinguishes memory held in AP-1 itself, in feedback loops, or in chromatin sites that AP-1 only opened (like defects holding domain walls).

title: Aging and pause-memory tests, with stability quantified
description: Vary the interval between the first and second stimulus (minutes to weeks) and the number of cell divisions between them, using single-cell tracking to see whether the second response is primed. Insert interruptions (e.g., a temporary signaling block mid-history) to see if cells recall them as dips in later response. Fit the decay to extract a retention half-life and an energy-barrier-like parameter, to say whether AP-1 memory lasts hours, days or generations.

title: First-order reversal curve (FORC) stimulation protocols
description: Drive cells to saturating AP-1 activation (e.g., high-dose TPA or serum/MAPK stimulation), withdraw to varied reversal levels, then re-stimulate, and read out chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene transcription at each step. Mapping which AP-1 sites and genes show path-dependent responses, with return-point memory versus simple relaxation, identifies a history-dependent hysteresis-like state and distinguishes it from the stimulus level alone.

title: Memory-and-rejuvenation pause experiments with decay-time series
description: Give a stimulus, pause or wash out for different durations, then restimulate and compare the response with naive cells, tracking FOS/JUN levels, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and enhancer accessibility over time. If the primed response persists long after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline, and the persistence is separable from slow relaxation (aging) by varying pause length and temperature, memory is more than a lingering transient.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics, 'Barkhausen' style
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN reporters and an AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells across repeated stimulations, resolving discrete bursts and enhancer switching events. Analyze the distribution of switching thresholds across cells, and test whether cells show bistability, with a Preisach-like decomposition into independent two-state loci, each with its own on/off thresholds.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation as an erasure/demagnetization test
description: Use degron-tagged or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 at defined times: during priming, during the memory interval, or only at restimulation. Compare this with erasure controls such as a decaying oscillating stimulus (an AC-field analogue), and read out chromatin state and gene expression. If AP-1 is needed only to write the memory, not to maintain it, it is an initiator; if removal during the interval erases the memory, it is a maintainer.

title: Site-specific mutation and epigenetic readout of pioneer-like AP-1 sites
description: Edit individual AP-1 motifs in memory-associated enhancers with CRISPR, or block them with dCas9, and measure whether priming-induced accessibility, H3K27ac, and enhanced re-induction are lost, using ATAC-seq, ChIP/CUT&Tag for histone marks and SWI/SNF (BAF), and nascent RNA. Combine with a chromatin-state perturbation, such as a BAF inhibitor, to test whether the stored thing is a self-sustaining chromatin state or only slow relaxation of AP-1 itself.

title: Rate-independent hysteresis of AP-1 target output
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemically induced ERK/JNK activation, or serum) up and down at progressively slower rates, and measure c-Fos/c-Jun levels, chromatin accessibility and target-gene transcription in single cells. A loop that persists in the quasi-static limit shows true rate-independent memory rather than kinetic lag from slow protein or mRNA turnover, and a lag-only model can be fitted and rejected.

title: Return-point memory via nested minor-loop stimulation
description: Drive cells with nested sequences of stimulus amplitudes (up to A1, down to B1, up to A2<A1, and so on) and read out AP-1 occupancy and reporter activity at each turning point. If the system keeps nested bookmarks of earlier extrema, and a larger excursion erases the smaller ones, that supports a Preisach-like population of AP-1 sites with distinct thresholds, as opposed to one global state variable.

title: Preisach-style decomposition of AP-1 enhancers from single-cell multiome data
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and RNA-seq after stimulation at graded doses and durations to estimate each enhancer's on and off thresholds, then test whether the whole-population response is reproduced by a distribution of independent bistable switches. Sites that open at a high threshold and close only at a much lower one are the memory elements, and a model built from these thresholds can be used to predict held-out stimulus histories.

title: Training-and-readout of amplitude memory plus erasure tests
description: Train cells with repeated pulses at a defined amplitude or frequency, rest them for varying times, and then probe with a test stimulus to see whether the response depends on the training amplitude, as in the Keim–Nagel protocol. Compare readout with a single probe versus repeated probes to test whether reading is destructive. Test erasure by AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) expression, by cell division or by a pulse larger than the trained one. Also test whether the memory depends on pioneer-like remodeling by perturbing SWI/SNF or histone modifiers.

title: Kovacs-like non-monotonic relaxation after a perturbation
description: Apply a step change in stimulus or signaling, such as a transient JNK/ERK inhibitor or activator pulse, and track AP-1 activity and chromatin state as they relax. Compare the trajectories of two preparations that reach the same instantaneous AP-1 level through different histories. Different later relaxation, such as non-monotonic overshoot, shows the cell carries hidden state variables beyond the AP-1 level, for example chromatin accessibility or partner-factor composition. Perturbing these hidden variables can then separate a switch-like mechanism from a phase-like one.

title: Stepwise 'demagnetization' of AP-1 chromatin memory
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, EGF, or TPA), progressively erase candidate memory carriers in graded steps: titrate dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS), degron-mediated depletion of FOS/JUN, then inhibitors of chromatin remodelers (BAF) or histone writers. Measure ATAC-seq accessibility and re-stimulation response after each step. A single straight-line decay to baseline implies one mechanism, while a kink implies stacked layers, for example a fast AP-1 protein-dependent component and a slow chromatin-based one.

title: Dating the imprint: acute vs. persistent AP-1 occupancy time course
description: Run CUT&RUN/ChIP for FOS/JUN family members, ATAC-seq, and H3K27ac at multiple times after stimulus withdrawal (hours to weeks). This separates sites where AP-1 itself persists, sites where accessibility persists after AP-1 is gone, and sites that fully revert. These sites correspond to 'viscous drift' versus a locked-in imprint, and the result dates each memory by its decay.

title: FORC-style reversal-history mapping of response thresholds
description: Subject cells to defined sequences of stimulus dose up and down (minor loops with varied reversal points), and read out single-cell AP-1 reporter activity and target gene transcription. Fit a Preisach-like model of independent bistable units, with each locus or cell having its own switching threshold, to test for hysteresis and return-point memory. Compare the distribution of thresholds with and without AP-1 perturbation to show whether AP-1 sets the hysteresis.

title: Aging and dwell-time dependence test
description: Vary the time between the priming stimulus and the challenge, and also the duration of priming, in fibroblasts, keratinocytes, or macrophages. Measure whether the secondary response magnitude or kinetics depends on the interval (aging, as in spin glasses) and whether it scales with priming dose and duration. Pair this with live imaging of an AP-1 reporter and single-cell lineage tracking to see whether memory is inherited through division.

title: Overwrite and conglomerate-style controls for causality
description: Use optogenetic or inducible AP-1 pulses delivered before versus after a separate chromatin-altering event (e.g., differentiation signal or inflammatory challenge) to test whether the AP-1-dependent accessibility predates or follows it. Also compare AP-1 motif sites across cell clones given independent priming histories: shared sites suggest a deterministic imprint, whereas randomly oriented, clone-specific sites suggest the signal arose later. Complement with motif mutagenesis by CRISPR at selected enhancers to test necessity for the remembered response.

title: Rate-dependent hysteresis of AP-1 target accessibility
description: Drive cells with a ramped up-and-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or PMA/ERK input controlling FOS/JUN) at several sweep rates, and measure ATAC-seq accessibility or reporter output of AP-1 target loci. Memory is the rate-independent loop area that persists as sweeps slow, which separates true bistable/epigenetic hysteresis from slow relaxation kinetics.

title: First-order reversal curves of single-cell AP-1 thresholds
description: Saturate AP-1 activity, reverse to varied intermediate input levels, then sweep up again while reading single-cell reporters of AP-1 targets. The resulting FORC map gives a census of up- and down-switching thresholds across cells or loci, testing whether the system is a set of bistable units with return-point memory.

title: Nested-history stack test (return-point memory)
description: Apply stimulus histories with nested peaks and reversals of different amplitudes, such as serial pulses of varying strength, then probe whether AP-1 binding and chromatin state recall only the extrema of the history and forget intermediate ones. Compare ChIP/CUT&RUN and transcriptional readouts across history orderings to show history-dependence beyond the current input.

title: Wipe and partial-erasure assays with AP-1 perturbation
description: After priming, erase memory by decaying oscillations of input (analogous to AC demagnetization), dominant-negative AP-1 (A-Fos), or degron-mediated depletion, at different times. Measure how fully accessibility and primed transcriptional responses on re-stimulation are lost, and whether defects persist partially, to show whether AP-1 is required for maintenance, not only for establishment.

title: Pinning-site analysis: pause-and-reheat memory and event noise
description: Map AP-1 motif and bound sites that remain accessible after stimulus removal (pioneer-like 'defects'), and mutate them by CRISPR to see whether memory is lost locally. Additionally, record single-locus live imaging or nascent transcription bursts for discrete switching events, and use a pause-then-resume protocol to test whether a transient exposure leaves a latent, recoverable signature on reactivation.

title: Long-timescale decay (viscosity) assay of AP-1 memory
description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or anisomycin) is removed, follow AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy by CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq, plus target transcription, over hours to weeks. Fit decay curves to separate true persistence from slow transients, as with magnetic viscosity, and test whether the 'forgetting clock' depends on dose, duration or cell division.

title: FORC-style stimulus-history mapping
description: Expose cells to a rise-then-reverse series of stimulus doses, varying the peak ('reversal') dose and the return dose, and read out single-cell AP-1 activity with a live reporter and downstream gene expression. The resulting 2D response map shows whether subpopulations act as hysteretic switches with distinct thresholds and biases, and whether the response depends on history beyond the current dose.

title: Return-point memory test with nested stimulus cycles
description: Apply a major stimulus loop, then a minor sub-cycle inside it, and check whether accessibility at AP-1 sites and gene output return exactly to the state at the turning point. Compare this with a decaying-amplitude 'AC demagnetization' protocol, which would erase the memory if the ledger lives in AP-1-dependent chromatin states.

title: Domain-wall versus defect: separating AP-1 from the sites it marks
description: Acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/auxin) after stimulation and measure whether accessibility and enhancer marks (H3K27ac) persist, which would place memory in the chromatin 'defects' rather than in AP-1 itself. Complement this with mutating or CRISPR-deleting individual AP-1 motifs and with pioneer-factor tests (e.g., nucleosome remodeling by BAF) to see which sites are self-sustaining.

title: Replay test: do the same sites reactivate on re-stimulation?
description: Like Barkhausen avalanches replaying the same sites, restimulate cells after a rest period and use single-cell multiome (scATAC and RNA) to ask whether the same loci open faster or more strongly in the same cells, compared with naive cells. Add lineage tracing or sibling-cell pairing to test inheritance through division, and use naive versus primed comparisons with AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) to show necessity.
